articles.title: Foguete dá ré? China consegue feito inédito ao fazer propulsor voltar e pousar em terra firme; VÍDEO | G1
articles.standfirst: tartup LandSpace recuperou o primeiro estágio do Zhuque-3 em sua segunda tentativa, aproximando a China da tecnologia de foguetes reutilizáveis desenvolvida por empresas como SpaceX e Blue Origin.
articles.summary: tartup LandSpace recuperou o primeiro estágio do Zhuque-3 em sua segunda tentativa, aproximando a China da tecnologia de foguetes reutilizáveis desenvolvida por empresas como SpaceX e Blue Origin.
articles.body:
A startup chinesa LandSpace conseguiu um feito inédito nesta quarta-feira (19): recuperou e pousou de ré, em terra firme, o primeiro estágio de seu foguete Zhuque-3. Veja o vídeo abaixo:

Segundo reportagem da Reuters, com a manobra, a empresa se tornou a primeira companhia privada chinesa a realizar esse tipo de pouso de um propulsor de classe orbital , aproximando o país da tecnologia de foguetes reutilizáveis dominada por empresas americanas como SpaceX e Blue Origin .

A capacidade de retornar, recuperar e reutilizar um propulsor é fundamental para reduzir custos e facilitar o lançamento de satélites em órbita, transformando a exploração espacial em um negócio comercialmente viável, semelhante à aviação civil.

O feito ocorreu na segunda tentativa da LandSpace de pousar o primeiro estágio do Zhuque-3, um foguete de aço inoxidável equipado com nove motores e apresentado pela empresa como a resposta chinesa ao Falcon 9, da SpaceX.

Com 66,1 metros de altura, o Zhuque-3 decolou da Zona-Piloto de Inovação Comercial Espacial de Dongfeng, no noroeste da China. O primeiro estágio — também chamado de propulsor — retornou a uma área de pouso na província de Gansu, a cerca de 390 quilômetros a sudeste da plataforma de lançamento, segundo a imprensa estatal chinesa.

China faz foguete pousar "de ré" em terra firme — Foto: Reprodução

O pouso deve aumentar a confiança dos investidores enquanto a LandSpace avança em seus planos de abrir capital no STAR Market, segmento de tecnologia da Bolsa de Xangai, escreveu a Reuters em sua reportagem.

A empresa pretende levantar 7,5 bilhões de yuans (US$ 1,11 bilhão ou R$ 5,73 bilhões) em uma oferta pública inicial de ações para financiar o desenvolvimento e ampliar seus serviços de lançamento de foguetes reutilizáveis.

Em junho, a empresa apresentou uma versão atualizada do prospecto de IPO à Bolsa de Xangai . No documento, afirmou que pretende se tornar lucrativa até 2029.

O lançamento desta quarta-feira marcou a quarta tentativa da China de recuperar um propulsor de foguete de classe orbital.

A LandSpace fez história em dezembro de 2025 ao se tornar a primeira empresa chinesa a realizar um teste de foguete reutilizável. O foguete entrou em órbita conforme o planejado, mas seu primeiro estágio não conseguiu concluir o pouso controlado.

Semanas depois, a China lançou o Long March 12A, desenvolvido pelo Estado, que também alcançou a órbita, mas não conseguiu recuperar o primeiro estágio.

Em julho, a China realizou com sucesso um teste experimental de recuperação de propulsor usando um sistema de captura por rede instalado em uma plataforma marítima. Com isso, tornou-se apenas o segundo país a conseguir pousar um foguete de classe orbital.

Diferentemente dos foguetes equipados com pernas de pouso retráteis, o Long March 10B reutilizável utiliza quatro ganchos leves para se conectar a cabos de aço instalados no sistema de rede da plataforma. Segundo Pequim, a inovação simplifica a estrutura do foguete, reduz seu peso e aumenta sua capacidade de carga.

articles.title: Google paga US$ 10 milhões por dados de companhia aérea falida para treinar IA | G1
articles.standfirst: Google paga US$ 10 milhões por dados da extinta Spirit Airlines para treinar IA, enquanto corrida do setor cria novos bilionários e movimenta bilhões em investimentos.
articles.summary: Google paga US$ 10 milhões por dados da extinta Spirit Airlines para treinar IA, enquanto corrida do setor cria novos bilionários e movimenta bilhões em investimentos.
articles.body:
Logotipo do Google é visto em escritório da empresa em Mountain View, na Califórnia — Foto: Paresh Dave/Reuters

O Google vai pagar US$ 10 milhões (R$ 51,7 milhões) pelos dados internos da Spirit Airlines , companhia aérea conhecida pelas passagens de baixo custo que encerrou as operações em maio após enfrentar preços elevados do combustível de aviação e uma pesada dívida.

Segundo reportagem da Forbes, o material será usado para treinar modelos de inteligência artificial da empresa.

Spirit Airlines — Foto: ASSOCIATED PRESS

O conjunto de dados inclui centenas de milhões de e-mails de funcionários , mensagens do Microsoft Teams , planilhas , calendários e informações operacionais . Todo o conteúdo será anonimizado antes da venda.

O valor dos dados foi suficiente para provocar uma disputa entre empresas. O Google venceu a startup de rotulagem de dados Mercor, que havia oferecido US$ 7,5 milhões (R$ 38,77 milhões).

Dados corporativos se tornaram especialmente valiosos para o treinamento de sistemas de inteligência artificial porque os laboratórios já haviam vasculhado praticamente toda a internet pública até o fim de 2024.

Empresas que encerraram suas atividades podem deixar para trás grandes volumes de informações digitais, como códigos, conversas por e-mail, mensagens no Slack e chamados de suporte de tecnologia, que ajudam a representar como funciona um ambiente de trabalho real.

Startups como SimpleClosure e Sunset, que auxiliam empresas no processo de encerramento das atividades, também passaram a oferecer a compra desses dados para treinamento de sistemas de IA .

articles.title: Ex-executivo diz que Meta deixou segurança infantil em segundo plano | G1
articles.standfirst: Depoimento ocorre em um julgamento considerado histórico nos EUA, em que estados acusam a empresa de promover dependência entre jovens e coletar dados de crianças de forma ilegal.
articles.summary: Em depoimento histórico, ex-diretor afirma que Mark Zuckerberg negligenciou a segurança infantil na Meta para priorizar o lucro e o engajamento de jovens.
articles.body:
Ex-diretor da Meta Arturo Bejar. — Foto: Jose Luis Magana/AP Photo

Um ex-diretor de engenharia da Meta Platforms testemunhou nesta quarta-feira (19) que o CEO, Mark Zuckerberg , foi responsável por criar uma cultura que pode ter levado a empresa a evitar sua responsabilidade de proteger crianças que usam o Facebook e o Instagram contra possíveis danos.

Arturo Bejar, que foi funcionário da empresa entre 2009 e 2015, afirmou que o presidente da Meta participava diretamente de grande parte das decisões. Segundo ele, a estrutura hierárquica da empresa fazia com que mudanças nos produtos só fossem implementadas mediante aprovação do CEO .

"Se Mark prioriza algo, montanhas se movem em poucos meses", disse Bejar.

Bejar é a primeira testemunha de um julgamento considerado histórico envolvendo acusações de uma coalizão de estados americanos . Os estados alegam que a Meta projetou suas plataformas para estimular o uso compulsivo entre usuários jovens e coletou ilegalmente dados de crianças menores de 13 anos.

Califórnia, Colorado, Kentucky e Nova Jersey acusam a Meta de desenvolver o Facebook e o Instagram de forma a incentivar o uso excessivo por jovens, contribuindo para problemas como ansiedade, depressão e até pensamentos suicidas. Os estados também afirmam que a empresa induziu consumidores ao erro sobre a segurança das plataformas.

Esses estados, juntamente com outros 25, também acusam a Meta de violar a legislação federal ao coletar e utilizar indevidamente dados pessoais de crianças em suas plataformas.

A Meta negou as acusações e argumentou que as opiniões de Bejar extrapolam o escopo de suas funções na empresa.

Bejar começou a depor na terça-feira, primeiro dia do julgamento, no tribunal federal de Oakland, na Califórnia.

O julgamento deve durar cerca de seis semanas, e a expectativa é que Zuckerberg também preste depoimento.

Mark Zuckerberg, CEO da Meta — Foto: ANDREW CABALLERO-REYNOLDS / AFP

Segurança era uma preocupação secundária

Bejar ajudou a conduzir pesquisas sobre a experiência de adolescentes no Instagram como integrante de uma equipe que analisava o impacto da plataforma no bem-estar dos usuários entre 2019 e 2021.

Desde então, ele se tornou um dos principais críticos das políticas de segurança da Meta para crianças. Em 2023, ao depor diante de uma comissão do Senado dos Estados Unidos , afirmou que a empresa tinha conhecimento de casos de assédio e de outros problemas enfrentados por adolescentes em suas plataformas, mas não adotou medidas suficientes para solucioná-los.

No depoimento desta quarta-feira, Bejar afirmou que a empresa utilizava indicadores como nível de engajamento e número de usuários ativos diários para avaliar e recompensar funcionários. Segundo ele, isso fazia com que o crescimento e a rentabilidade recebessem mais atenção do que a segurança dos usuários.

Ele também afirmou que uma ferramenta criada para incentivar pausas no uso dos aplicativos, frequentemente citada pela Meta em sua defesa, teria sido "projetada para falhar". Segundo Bejar, o recurso não vem ativado por padrão e os lembretes são fáceis de ignorar.

"Tudo depende de como o tempo de desenvolvimento dos produtos é distribuído", disse ele. "Nesse contexto, a segurança sempre ficou em segundo plano."

Bejar também afirmou que a Meta tinha tecnologia para identificar usuários suspeitos de terem menos de 13 anos e exigir verificações adicionais de idade. Segundo ele, a empresa optava por não agir de forma ampla diante do problema, adotando uma postura que classificou como de "não pergunte, não conte", por considerar essa estratégia financeiramente vantajosa no longo prazo.

"Onde estão as crianças de hoje estão também os usuários do futuro", disse ele.

Especialistas afirmam que este julgamento representa o maior teste judicial já realizado sobre os efeitos das redes sociais entre os jovens.

A Meta enfrenta milhares de processos semelhantes relacionados a supostos danos causados a crianças. Bejar atuou como testemunha em três dos casos que chegaram a julgamento até agora. Um deles, movido pelo estado do Novo México, terminou com a imposição de US$ 942 milhões em indenizações e multas, além de uma ordem judicial determinando mudanças nas plataformas da empresa no estado.

Um ex-diretor de engenharia da Meta Platforms testemunhou nesta quarta-feira (19) que o CEO, Mark Zuckerberg , foi responsável por criar uma cultura que pode ter levado a empresa a evitar sua responsabilidade de proteger crianças que usam o Facebook e o Instagram contra possíveis danos.

Arturo Bejar, que foi funcionário da empresa entre 2009 e 2015, afirmou que o presidente da Meta participava diretamente de grande parte das decisões. Segundo ele, a estrutura hierárquica da empresa fazia com que mudanças nos produtos só fossem implementadas mediante aprovação do CEO .
"Se Mark prioriza algo, montanhas se movem em poucos meses", disse Bejar.

Bejar é a primeira testemunha de um julgamento considerado histórico envolvendo acusações de uma coalizão de estados americanos . Os estados alegam que a Meta projetou suas plataformas para estimular o uso compulsivo entre usuários jovens e coletou ilegalmente dados de crianças menores de 13 anos.

Califórnia, Colorado, Kentucky e Nova Jersey acusam a Meta de desenvolver o Facebook e o Instagram de forma a incentivar o uso excessivo por jovens, contribuindo para problemas como ansiedade, depressão e até pensamentos suicidas. Os estados também afirmam que a empresa induziu consumidores ao erro sobre a segurança das plataformas.
Esses estados, juntamente com outros 25, também acusam a Meta de violar a legislação federal ao coletar e utilizar indevidamente dados pessoais de crianças em suas plataformas.
A Meta negou as acusações e argumentou que as opiniões de Bejar extrapolam o escopo de suas funções na empresa.
Bejar começou a depor na terça-feira, primeiro dia do julgamento, no tribunal federal de Oakland, na Califórnia.
O julgamento deve durar cerca de seis semanas, e a expectativa é que Zuckerberg também preste depoimento.

articles.title: Austrália aprova lei que cobra gigantes de tecnologia por notícias | G1
articles.standfirst: Nova lei australiana prevê que plataformas desembolsem 2,5% da receita publicitária se não fecharem acordos com veículos de imprensa.
articles.summary: Nova lei australiana prevê que plataformas desembolsem 2,5% da receita publicitária se não fecharem acordos com veículos de imprensa.
articles.body:
A Austrália aprovou nesta quinta-feira (20) uma lei que pode obrigar grandes empresas de tecnologia a pagar milhões de dólares australianos a veículos de imprensa do país caso não façam acordos comerciais para financiar a produção de notícias.

A chamada News Bargaining Incentive prevê uma cobrança equivalente a 2,5% da receita de publicidade das plataformas que se enquadrarem na regra e não cumprirem as exigências previstas na legislação.

A medida vale para empresas com serviços relevantes de busca ou redes sociais na Austrália e receita anual de publicidade no país superior a 250 milhões de dólares australianos (cerca de US$ 178 milhões),

Google, Meta, TikTok e LinkedIn estão entre os alvos

A cobrança poderá atingir empresas como Google, da Alphabet, Meta, TikTok e LinkedIn, da Microsoft.

'Não sabia o quanto minha filha era viciada': brasileiros contam como foi a proibição de redes sociais na Austrália

O dinheiro arrecadado será destinado a veículos de imprensa australianos. O governo argumenta que as plataformas se beneficiam do conteúdo jornalístico ao utilizá-lo para aumentar o engajamento dos usuários e, consequentemente, a receita publicitária.

Marco civil da internet: como EUA e Europa tratam as 'big techs' — Foto: BBC/Getty Images

As empresas, porém, podem evitar a cobrança se fecharem acordos comerciais com veículos de comunicação.

Empresas terão de fechar acordos com ao menos 8 veículos

Para escapar da cobrança, as plataformas deverão firmar acordos com pelo menos oito diferentes empresas de mídia até o fim de seu período de prestação de contas.

Os contratos precisam financiar a produção de notícias ou estar relacionados à disponibilização de conteúdo jornalístico produzido pelos veículos nas plataformas.

O valor pago nos acordos será descontado da quantia que a empresa teria de pagar como cobrança.

A legislação ainda estabelece incentivos diferentes de acordo com o tamanho do veículo: gastos com grandes empresas de mídia terão um abatimento de 150%, enquanto acordos com veículos pequenos e médios terão abatimento de 200%.

Cada contrato individual, porém, poderá representar no máximo 25% do valor total da cobrança à qual a plataforma estaria sujeita.

Austrália já havia criado regras para plataformas

A nova legislação amplia a pressão da Austrália sobre as grandes empresas de tecnologia para que compartilhem parte da receita gerada com a distribuição de conteúdo jornalístico.

O governo australiano afirmou que a aprovação da lei deixa claro para as plataformas que elas devem buscar acordos comerciais com os veículos de imprensa.

A medida foi aprovada um dia depois de o Parlamento australiano também aprovar restrições à publicidade de apostas.

articles.title: They lost weight with a GLP-1. Then their spending changed in ways they never saw coming.
articles.summary: Paying for GLP-1 medications is just the beginning. The drugs can reshape how people spend and save — and even what they’re willing to splurge on.
articles.body:
As Ozempic's popularity soared in the early 2020s, its eye-popping cost — more than $1,000 for a month's supply, in some cases — made headlines . With more GLP-1 options now on the market, broader insurance coverage for the drugs to treat additional conditions and the proliferation of cheaper compounded versions, prices have slowly begun to come down, putting the medications within reach for more people.

For those self-paying for the weight loss versions of the medications, one month of Wegovy now costs between $349 and $499, depending on the dose, while Zepbound's prices now range from $299 to $449 for four weeks of doses.

Meanwhile, GLP-1 drugs are changing the way people shop and eat. They helped fuel the protein-maxxing craze , triggered what some have called a " structural disruption" to the food and beverage industry, and even changed what ends up in people's grocery carts. Within six months of starting the medications, people cut their supermarket spending by 5.3% , while savory snack purchases dropped by more than 11%.

I've been reporting on GLP-1 medications for years now and have interviewed dozens of people who have taken the medication. If there's one thing that's become clear, it's that when the medications work as hoped, they set in motion a cascade of changes in people's lives. Controlled blood sugar and weight loss are just the beginning for many people, who find their cravings for less nutritious snacks fade away, their desire to drink alcohol ebbs and their healthier habits and routines become easier to stick to.

The same goes for their personal finances: The cost of GLP-1s themselves is only the first of many budgetary changes that come with the weekly shot.

The associate dean saving thousands on takeout

When I first spoke to Michael Donnelly-Boylen in 2025, the 52-year-old had a new lease on life — literally. He'd felt so long that he was fighting a losing battle against his health issues that he was " preparing for death ," Donnelly-Boylen told me. Meanwhile, he and his husband were spending as much as $75 a day on delivery orders for lunch, dinner and sometimes breakfast. On the rare occasion that he or his husband did go grocery shopping, their haul was "almost entirely snacks," Donnelly-Boylen says. "Maybe we'd buy eggs and milk, but a lot of that was just to bake goodies; it wasn't for good use."

Then he started taking Mounjaro — and his appetite, eating habits and spending changed.

Now, Donnelly-Boylen only uses meal delivery services to order healthy, protein-rich foods to his hotel when he travels. That amounts to about $2,000 saved per month. It more than covers the "bougie" groceries he buys now (though, he does still get them via Instacart — "I don't like the carts and the people, it's just madness," Donnelly-Boylen says). The foods he stocks in his fridge aren't cheap, but they're packed with nutrients and contain far less fat and fewer ultraprocessed ingredients than what Donnelly-Boylen used to eat. "If you told me two years ago that my favorite snack would be cottage cheese with berries, I would've told you you're crazy — but that's my life these days," he says.

Donnelly-Boylen was also able to quit taking other prescriptions, including his blood pressure medication, and he's lost virtually all interest in alcohol (which he previously spent about $200 a month on). But of course there are new expenses — including an air fryer, blender and a soft serve machine to support his new healthy cooking habits.

Then there were the clothes. As Donnelly-Boylen started losing weight, his clothing size quickly went down. And each new size meant buying at least enough new clothes to look professional at work events. Eventually, though, he reached his husband's lower weight and started wearing his hand-me-downs. Donnelly-Boylen's husband had gone up in size, so he started taking a GLP-1 drug too and began losing weight. So the pair keep about half of their clothes in a storage unit. "Now I shop in the storage unit," says Donnelly-Boylen.

In total, the savings — especially on takeout — mean that Donnelly-Boylen's monthly spending is down by almost $2,000. But there's a catch. While his own GLP-1 is covered by insurance and costs him just $25 a month, his husband's medication is not, and costs $330 per month. "The savings that I got, a lot of that is being eaten by [the cost of] his medication," says Donnelly-Boylen.

The stroke survivor spending on travel and fashion

After ShantaQuilette Carter-Williams suffered a stroke in her early 40s, her doctor said her weight was putting her life at risk and recommended a GLP-1. But her insurance wouldn't cover it, so she'd have to pay $1,600 a month out of pocket. "I was like, 'I'm gonna die because I can't afford that,'" Carter-Williams told Yahoo in a previous interview . But then she found out she had type 2 diabetes, a diagnosis that many GLP-1 users have told me is both a blessing and a curse. No one wants a potentially life-threatening illness, but it did mean her insurance would cover Ozempic, with a co-pay of just $25.

Food has always been — and remains — an important way for Carter-Williams and her family to connect. But instead of DoorDashing meals, regularly eating three-course dinners out with her husband and getting snacks delivered from grocery stores, Carter-Williams now shops at Sprouts and has memberships to healthier meal delivery services, including Gardencup . The individual grocery items might be more expensive, but she estimates she still saves several hundred dollars a month on food just by eating less. Carter-Williams and her husband still treat themselves to dinner out, but she says, "My appetite is not as big, and it's more managed."

One look at Carter-Williams on social media and it's clear: She's a woman with her own style. "The girlies love the clothes; bigger or smaller, that's right," she says. But plus-size clothing brands were often expensive. After taking a GLP-1 (Carter-Williams went off hers in February of 2025, but has maintained her weight loss), she can now buy clothes from more affordable retailers. "I can shop at a lot of different stores economically that I couldn't before," allowing her to buy more items she loves without a bigger hit to her wallet.

Along with new shopping destinations, Carter-Williams's improved health has made her want to travel to new places. With her weight and key health measures under control, she was able to take fewer medications and wanted to make the most of her newfound energy. First stop: Costa Rica for zip-lining and canyoning (though, she later realized, these adrenaline-pumping activities are still high-risk for stroke survivors and those with heart conditions).

Surprisingly, traveling to new parts of the world hasn't increased her vacation spending. "When we traveled internationally, we used to get business class so you could lay down," Carter-Williams says. "But that costs a lot more, right? And I would have to do that because I couldn't fit comfortably in a [standard cabin] chair." A first-class seat on a flight to Turkey earlier this year would have cost Carter-Williams $11,000, she says. But she opted for economy. "I can literally comfortably stretch my legs out and do all those things that I didn't realize [were] an issue until they weren't an issue," she says.

The plus-size influencer who's been freed from the 'fat tax'

Andy Neal rose to internet fame for taking " stupid hikes for [his] stupid mental health. " His therapist had recommended he take up hiking to help him recover from his binge eating disorder. Neal is also a filmmaker. His footage of the gorgeous trails he was walking, paired with his mildly self-deprecating humor and totally unironic joy, caught the attention of major brands, including Nike and REI. That marked the launch of a new phase of his career as a plus-size model and influencer. But when brands weren't giving him free items, "the plus-size stores were so prohibitively expensive," Neal tells Yahoo.

Despite his active lifestyle, Neal's weight remained consistently high. Long hikes left him debilitatingly sore. By adding time in the gym and making changes to his diet, he managed to lose 40 pounds, but the scale wouldn't drop below 360 pounds. After some initial skepticism, Neal decided to try a GLP-1 medication in June 2025. Within six months, he'd lost 100 pounds.

The medication costs him $199 for a four-week supply of shots. "We definitely had to make some adjustments" in terms of finances, Neal says. He and his wife combed through their subscriptions — canceling streaming services they didn't use much and Neal's $60-per-month LinkedIn Premium subscription, which served its purpose maybe once a year — to make room in their budget for his tirzepatide. The cost has since gone up for his dose, but "it's fine — the way it's changed my life, I don't mind paying for it," Neal says.

He estimates that the medication has slashed his personal food spending by about half. But, with a growing 13-year-old daughter who's into basketball, the family's overall meal budget is about the same — it just consists of a lot more healthy groceries and far fewer snacks or takeout meals. And they still pay for their $110 monthly gym membership, "but I'm using it much more consistently," says Neal. "I used to say it was a monthly fat tax."

As for his wardrobe spending? Like Carter-Williams, Neal is spending less per item, but he hasn't exactly saved money. "My wife gets onto me because, before, I couldn't go into a store and buy whatever I wanted, so I'm trying things stylewise that I couldn't before," Neal says. As a result, he's spending several hundred dollars a month on clothes, including suits and dress clothes that he needs to wear to influencer conferences.

In total, his monthly spending has increased slightly — by about $70 — since starting a GLP-1. "I do it gladly …I know it's privileged, but these are costs that, when you talk to your doctor, nobody talks to you about," says Neal.

The cookbook author investing in her health — without giving up the things she loves

Suzy Chase lives in New York City — which, in her words, means that life is expensive any way you slice it. But she's always paid for her beloved workout classes because they are "my social time, my therapy, my everything, all wrapped into one," Chase previously told Yahoo. The one thing they didn't do for her, however, was help her lose weight. And when menopause and the COVID-19 pandemic hit at the same time, Chase's weight crept up.

Then she learned about the GLP-1, Zepbound. The weekly injections helped Chase lose 50 pounds and set the 59-year-old's sights on a new goal: "training for 80." She didn't qualify for insurance coverage, so Chase was at first paying $1,080 per month out of pocket for her medication. Yet even with the added cost of the medication, Chase says being on a GLP-1 hasn't otherwise changed how she spends her money or time. She still goes to the same two workout studios and pays the same amount for the classes, "but now I'm seeing my hard work paying off," she says.

As a cookbook author and podcaster , Chase has never scrimped on groceries, and she still doesn't. But her shopping and eating habits have changed. Instead of roaming the center aisles of the grocery store where the snacks live, "I am definitely shopping the perimeter of the grocery store a lot more," Chase says. "I'm not saving money, [I've] just pivoted from a lot of red meat to vegetarian and pescatarian foods." The biggest adjustment to her budget was replacing her wardrobe — at a cost of about $3,500 in total — as her size changed. "I've had to get everything new, but it's been slowly over time," she says.

Chase eventually switched to getting her Zepbound from Lilly Direct, where her 2.5-milligram dose costs $299 per month. And she's figured out a way to maintain her weight and her account balance: Chase now spaces her doses out every 15 days (instead of every seven), bringing her prorated monthly cost down to about $150, she estimates. "Tweaking my dose has been really good for the budget," she says. "I sort of changed my mindset, and now I think about [Zepbound] as a support tool and not the solution. Spacing my doses and retraining how I think about food has made a world of difference."

The teacher paying for her GLP-1 with takeout savings

After caring for her grandmother in the final days of her life as she suffered from complications of rheumatoid arthritis, Cassandra Smith knew she didn't want to face the same fate. Smith had been diagnosed with the autoimmune disease by age 30 and was already dealing with debilitating flare-ups. Her doctor told her that inflammation from being overweight was only making it worse. Starting a Mediterranean diet helped, but it didn't get Smith anywhere near a healthy BMI.

She knew that a GLP-1 drug would help her lose weight , which would, in turn, help with the symptoms of her autoimmune condition. But the medications aren't approved to treat rheumatoid arthritis, so her insurance wouldn't cover them. Smith instead gets her compounded tirzepatide from a telehealth company and pays $399 a month for it. That's no small sum, but Smith told herself, "You're not eating out, you're cooking at home and you're going to pay for your medicine," she tells Yahoo. "I basically took the money [for the GLP-1] out of my eating-out habit."

Smith cut what she spent dining out with her daughter from about $200 a month to about $50. When the pair goes to their favorite Chinese restaurant, they each order a $5 kids' meal. "The lady there is even like, 'Oh, ya'll want the kids' meal?' She knows the drill," Smith says.

Her grocery bill has also shrunk, from $550 a month to $320. "My bill has definitely gone down because I don't get all the snacks, I don't get all the different cereals, or all the flour, oil — all the extra stuff you have to do to basically eat unhealthy," she says. Smith's preferred proteins are fish and red meat, which can be pricey. But otherwise, she tries to eat raw fruits and vegetables most of the time. "I don't buy as many ingredients anymore," she says. "The ingredients I am buying are still a little expensive, but I don't have to add anything additional to them."

Some of Smith's expenses have increased, though. Before taking a GLP-1 drug, she didn't have a workout routine. Now Smith goes to Pilates at least once a week and has joined a gym. She also bought a membership to a "jump house" for kids — where she sometimes jumps alongside her daughter.

Like exercise, fashion was a $0 line item in Smith's monthly budget because she "hated" clothes before starting a GLP-1 medication. But losing weight has led to investing in a new, colorful wardrobe to match her church choir's weekly themes.

On the whole, Smith says she's still saving several hundred dollars a month. "If I say I'm not going to do something, I'm not going to do it," she says. And for the moments when she's tempted to let her resolve soften, Smith has "a little 5-year-old accountability partner" in her daughter. "It's kind of hard to do the wrong thing when she's always with me."

On the rare occasion that he or his husband did go grocery shopping, their haul was "almost entirely snacks," Donnelly-Boylen says. "Maybe we'd buy eggs and milk, but a lot of that was just to bake goodies; it wasn't for good use."
Then he started taking Mounjaro — and his appetite, eating habits and spending changed.

Now, Donnelly-Boylen only uses meal delivery services to order healthy, protein-rich foods to his hotel when he travels. That amounts to about $2,000 saved per month. It more than covers the "bougie" groceries he buys now (though, he does still get them via Instacart — "I don't like the carts and the people, it's just madness," Donnelly-Boylen says). The foods he stocks in his fridge aren't cheap, but they're packed with nutrients and contain far less fat and fewer ultraprocessed ingredients than what Donnelly-Boylen used to eat. "If you told me two years ago that my favorite snack would be cottage cheese with berries, I would've told you you're crazy — but that's my life these days," he says.

Donnelly-Boylen was also able to quit taking other prescriptions, including his blood pressure medication, and he's lost virtually all interest in alcohol (which he previously spent about $200 a month on). But of course there are new expenses — including an air fryer, blender and a soft serve machine to support his new healthy cooking habits.

Then there were the clothes. As Donnelly-Boylen started losing weight, his clothing size quickly went down. And each new size meant buying at least enough new clothes to look professional at work events. Eventually, though, he reached his husband's lower weight and started wearing his hand-me-downs. Donnelly-Boylen's husband had gone up in size, so he started taking a GLP-1 drug too and began losing weight. So the pair keep about half of their clothes in a storage unit. "Now I shop in the storage unit," says Donnelly-Boylen.

In total, the savings — especially on takeout — mean that Donnelly-Boylen's monthly spending is down by almost $2,000. But there's a catch. While his own GLP-1 is covered by insurance and costs him just $25 a month, his husband's medication is not, and costs $330 per month. "The savings that I got, a lot of that is being eaten by [the cost of] his medication," says Donnelly-Boylen.
The stroke survivor spending on travel and fashion

After ShantaQuilette Carter-Williams suffered a stroke in her early 40s, her doctor said her weight was putting her life at risk and recommended a GLP-1. But her insurance wouldn't cover it, so she'd have to pay $1,600 a month out of pocket. "I was like, 'I'm gonna die because I can't afford that,'" Carter-Williams told Yahoo in a previous interview . But then she found out she had type 2 diabetes, a diagnosis that many GLP-1 users have told me is both a blessing and a curse. No one wants a potentially life-threatening illness, but it did mean her insurance would cover Ozempic, with a co-pay of just $25.

Food has always been — and remains — an important way for Carter-Williams and her family to connect. But instead of DoorDashing meals, regularly eating three-course dinners out with her husband and getting snacks delivered from grocery stores, Carter-Williams now shops at Sprouts and has memberships to healthier meal delivery services, including Gardencup . The individual grocery items might be more expensive, but she estimates she still saves several hundred dollars a month on food just by eating less. Carter-Williams and her husband still treat themselves to dinner out, but she says, "My appetite is not as big, and it's more managed."

One look at Carter-Williams on social media and it's clear: She's a woman with her own style. "The girlies love the clothes; bigger or smaller, that's right," she says. But plus-size clothing brands were often expensive. After taking a GLP-1 (Carter-Williams went off hers in February of 2025, but has maintained her weight loss), she can now buy clothes from more affordable retailers. "I can shop at a lot of different stores economically that I couldn't before," allowing her to buy more items she loves without a bigger hit to her wallet.

Along with new shopping destinations, Carter-Williams's improved health has made her want to travel to new places. With her weight and key health measures under control, she was able to take fewer medications and wanted to make the most of her newfound energy. First stop: Costa Rica for zip-lining and canyoning (though, she later realized, these adrenaline-pumping activities are still high-risk for stroke survivors and those with heart conditions).

Surprisingly, traveling to new parts of the world hasn't increased her vacation spending. "When we traveled internationally, we used to get business class so you could lay down," Carter-Williams says. "But that costs a lot more, right? And I would have to do that because I couldn't fit comfortably in a [standard cabin] chair." A first-class seat on a flight to Turkey earlier this year would have cost Carter-Williams $11,000, she says. But she opted for economy. "I can literally comfortably stretch my legs out and do all those things that I didn't realize [were] an issue until they weren't an issue," she says.
The plus-size influencer who's been freed from the 'fat tax'

Andy Neal rose to internet fame for taking " stupid hikes for [his] stupid mental health. " His therapist had recommended he take up hiking to help him recover from his binge eating disorder. Neal is also a filmmaker. His footage of the gorgeous trails he was walking, paired with his mildly self-deprecating humor and totally unironic joy, caught the attention of major brands, including Nike and REI. That marked the launch of a new phase of his career as a plus-size model and influencer. But when brands weren't giving him free items, "the plus-size stores were so prohibitively expensive," Neal tells Yahoo.

Despite his active lifestyle, Neal's weight remained consistently high. Long hikes left him debilitatingly sore. By adding time in the gym and making changes to his diet, he managed to lose 40 pounds, but the scale wouldn't drop below 360 pounds. After some initial skepticism, Neal decided to try a GLP-1 medication in June 2025. Within six months, he'd lost 100 pounds.

The medication costs him $199 for a four-week supply of shots. "We definitely had to make some adjustments" in terms of finances, Neal says. He and his wife combed through their subscriptions — canceling streaming services they didn't use much and Neal's $60-per-month LinkedIn Premium subscription, which served its purpose maybe once a year — to make room in their budget for his tirzepatide. The cost has since gone up for his dose, but "it's fine — the way it's changed my life, I don't mind paying for it," Neal says.

He estimates that the medication has slashed his personal food spending by about half. But, with a growing 13-year-old daughter who's into basketball, the family's overall meal budget is about the same — it just consists of a lot more healthy groceries and far fewer snacks or takeout meals. And they still pay for their $110 monthly gym membership, "but I'm using it much more consistently," says Neal. "I used to say it was a monthly fat tax."

As for his wardrobe spending? Like Carter-Williams, Neal is spending less per item, but he hasn't exactly saved money. "My wife gets onto me because, before, I couldn't go into a store and buy whatever I wanted, so I'm trying things stylewise that I couldn't before," Neal says. As a result, he's spending several hundred dollars a month on clothes, including suits and dress clothes that he needs to wear to influencer conferences.

In total, his monthly spending has increased slightly — by about $70 — since starting a GLP-1. "I do it gladly …I know it's privileged, but these are costs that, when you talk to your doctor, nobody talks to you about," says Neal.
The cookbook author investing in her health — without giving up the things she loves

Suzy Chase lives in New York City — which, in her words, means that life is expensive any way you slice it. But she's always paid for her beloved workout classes because they are "my social time, my therapy, my everything, all wrapped into one," Chase previously told Yahoo. The one thing they didn't do for her, however, was help her lose weight. And when menopause and the COVID-19 pandemic hit at the same time, Chase's weight crept up.

Then she learned about the GLP-1, Zepbound. The weekly injections helped Chase lose 50 pounds and set the 59-year-old's sights on a new goal: "training for 80." She didn't qualify for insurance coverage, so Chase was at first paying $1,080 per month out of pocket for her medication. Yet even with the added cost of the medication, Chase says being on a GLP-1 hasn't otherwise changed how she spends her money or time. She still goes to the same two workout studios and pays the same amount for the classes, "but now I'm seeing my hard work paying off," she says.

As a cookbook author and podcaster , Chase has never scrimped on groceries, and she still doesn't. But her shopping and eating habits have changed. Instead of roaming the center aisles of the grocery store where the snacks live, "I am definitely shopping the perimeter of the grocery store a lot more," Chase says. "I'm not saving money, [I've] just pivoted from a lot of red meat to vegetarian and pescatarian foods." The biggest adjustment to her budget was replacing her wardrobe — at a cost of about $3,500 in total — as her size changed. "I've had to get everything new, but it's been slowly over time," she says.

Chase eventually switched to getting her Zepbound from Lilly Direct, where her 2.5-milligram dose costs $299 per month. And she's figured out a way to maintain her weight and her account balance: Chase now spaces her doses out every 15 days (instead of every seven), bringing her prorated monthly cost down to about $150, she estimates. "Tweaking my dose has been really good for the budget," she says. "I sort of changed my mindset, and now I think about [Zepbound] as a support tool and not the solution. Spacing my doses and retraining how I think about food has made a world of difference."
The teacher paying for her GLP-1 with takeout savings

After caring for her grandmother in the final days of her life as she suffered from complications of rheumatoid arthritis, Cassandra Smith knew she didn't want to face the same fate. Smith had been diagnosed with the autoimmune disease by age 30 and was already dealing with debilitating flare-ups. Her doctor told her that inflammation from being overweight was only making it worse. Starting a Mediterranean diet helped, but it didn't get Smith anywhere near a healthy BMI.

She knew that a GLP-1 drug would help her lose weight , which would, in turn, help with the symptoms of her autoimmune condition. But the medications aren't approved to treat rheumatoid arthritis, so her insurance wouldn't cover them. Smith instead gets her compounded tirzepatide from a telehealth company and pays $399 a month for it. That's no small sum, but Smith told herself, "You're not eating out, you're cooking at home and you're going to pay for your medicine," she tells Yahoo. "I basically took the money [for the GLP-1] out of my eating-out habit."

Smith cut what she spent dining out with her daughter from about $200 a month to about $50. When the pair goes to their favorite Chinese restaurant, they each order a $5 kids' meal. "The lady there is even like, 'Oh, ya'll want the kids' meal?' She knows the drill," Smith says.

Her grocery bill has also shrunk, from $550 a month to $320. "My bill has definitely gone down because I don't get all the snacks, I don't get all the different cereals, or all the flour, oil — all the extra stuff you have to do to basically eat unhealthy," she says. Smith's preferred proteins are fish and red meat, which can be pricey. But otherwise, she tries to eat raw fruits and vegetables most of the time. "I don't buy as many ingredients anymore," she says. "The ingredients I am buying are still a little expensive, but I don't have to add anything additional to them."

Some of Smith's expenses have increased, though. Before taking a GLP-1 drug, she didn't have a workout routine. Now Smith goes to Pilates at least once a week and has joined a gym. She also bought a membership to a "jump house" for kids — where she sometimes jumps alongside her daughter.

Like exercise, fashion was a $0 line item in Smith's monthly budget because she "hated" clothes before starting a GLP-1 medication. But losing weight has led to investing in a new, colorful wardrobe to match her church choir's weekly themes.

On the whole, Smith says she's still saving several hundred dollars a month. "If I say I'm not going to do something, I'm not going to do it," she says. And for the moments when she's tempted to let her resolve soften, Smith has "a little 5-year-old accountability partner" in her daughter. "It's kind of hard to do the wrong thing when she's always with me."

articles.title: Jannik Sinner to miss US Open tennis major due to knee injury
articles.summary: Five-time major champion Sinner, who won the US Open in 2024, will not be competing at Flushing Meadows this year.
articles.body:
Top-ranked Jannik Sinner has withdrawn from the US Open, unable to recover from a right knee injury that has sidelined him since winning the Wimbledon title.

Sinner beat Alexander Zverev last month for his second straight title at the All England Club, but then pulled out of the hard-court tournaments in Montreal and Cincinnati that serve as a warm-up for the US Open.

The 25-year-old Italian told social media on Friday that he won’t be ready when the main draw begins on August 30 .

“Even though I have been working hard with my team and my medical staff, we have now had to make the difficult decision that I will not be able to compete at the US Open this year,” Sinner posted on X.

“We have been back on court in Monte Carlo over the last couple of days and have realised that I still need more time to recover from my right knee issue.

“I’m obviously very sad and disappointed, as New York has a special place in my heart. I was very much looking forward to coming back and playing in the electric atmosphere in front of the great fans there.”

Sinner was the 2024 US Open champion and lost to Carlos Alcaraz in last year’s final.

Alcaraz posted on social media on Thursday that he would be ready to play in New York after being out of action since April because of a right wrist injury.

The rivalry between them has dominated men’s tennis in recent years and they met in the last three Grand Slam finals last year. Alcaraz won the most recent with his four-set victory in New York.

That ended Sinner’s title reign after beating Taylor Fritz in straight sets in the 2024 final.

Sinner is 44-3 with six titles this year. He had a stunning collapse at the French Open, blowing a two-set lead while struggling in the heat in his second-round match against Juan Manuel Cerundolo. He then sat out until Wimbledon, where his victory gave him five Grand Slam titles.

It will be the first time Sinner has missed a Grand Slam tournament since making his major debut at the US Open in 2019.

articles.title: US judge strikes down Trump immigrant visa ban affecting 75 countries
articles.summary: A federal judge in Manhattan ruled against the State Department’s suspension of immigrant visas.
articles.body:
A United States judge has struck down a policy introduced by the administration of President Donald Trump suspending the issuance of immigrant visas to applicants from 75 countries, saying the policy exceeded Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s statutory authority.

Judge Jeannette Vargas of Manhattan said in her ruling on Friday in the Southern District of New York that the policy was “patently unlawful” and conflicted with federal immigration law, which explicitly stripped the secretary of state of authority over consular officers’ adjudication of immigrant visas.

list 1 of 3 Is Trump planning an ‘Africa visa ban’?

list 2 of 3 Why are some African countries banning US citizens from entry?

list 3 of 3 Why are some African-Americans moving to Africa?

“The Policy, which categorically prohibits the issuance of immigrant visas based upon the nationality of the applicant, represents a direct abrogation of this statutory scheme,” she wrote.

Vargas, an appointee of Democratic former President Joe Biden, issued the ruling in a lawsuit filed by immigrant rights groups Catholic Legal Immigration Network and African Communities Together, along with applicants for immigrant visas and US citizens sponsoring family members from the designated countries.

The suspension, which took effect in January of this year, affected applicants from Latin American countries including Brazil , Colombia and Uruguay; Balkan nations such as Bosnia and Albania; South Asian countries like Pakistan and Bangladesh; and many nations in Africa , the Middle East and the Caribbean.

The Department of State said applicants from those countries were “at a high risk for becoming a public charge and recourse to local, state and federal government resources in the United States”.

President Donald Trump has pursued an aggressive immigration crackdown during his presidency that he argues is aimed at improving domestic security. According to the Center for Constitutional Rights, the freeze was one of several restrictions the administration has imposed in rapid succession, following a broader travel ban covering 39 countries that took effect January 1, and a pause on diversity visa issuance in late December.

Rights groups have suggested that the crackdown violates free speech and due process rights, particularly for minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling.

The State Department has not yet commented on the ruling.

articles.title: Northamptoshire Dogfather set for Strictly after stroke recovery
articles.summary: Graeme Hall from the Channel 5 series 'Dogs Behaving (Very) Badly' is joining Strictly Come Dancing.
articles.body:
TV dog trainer Graeme Hall says it is a "dream come true" to be on Strictly Come Dancing, after a stroke made him think he would never dance again.

The Brackley-based Dogs Behaving (Very) Badly star will appear on the BBC One show when it launches in September, despite giving up dancing after falling ill in 2019.

Known as the Dogfather on the Channel 5 television series, Hall has previously danced in local competitions, including Strictly Northampton.

"There are not a lot of people in the world that have had the chance to do this. So I'm just going to love every minute, enjoy it for what it is and hope it keeps going as long as possible," he said.

Speaking to Bernie Keith on BBC Radio Northampton , Hall said he did not expect to dance again after having a stroke caused by a hole in the heart.

"I never got back to dancing, I just thought, 'well that was a bit of fun'... and that was that.

"I put the dance bag in the loft. It's been with me through three house moves," he added.

Now having made a full recovery, Hall has dusted off his dancing kit and is "loving the experience".

Hall will only find out who his dance partner is during the launch show on 26 September 2026.

He said: "The celebrities are all really nice people, it's going to be great but it's not going to be easy because they actually, as far as I can tell, are quite good at dancing."

Hall is also known for fronting The Dog Hospital and his contributions to BBC radio programmes, ITV's This Morning, and writing a regular column for the Times.

He has written books including The Ultimate Kid's Guide to Dogs and previously made a cameo appearance in the hit drama All Creatures Great and Small.

articles.title: Red Lobster brings back Endless Shrimp after promotion helped push chain toward bankruptcy
articles.summary: Red Lobster rebuilt its Endless Shrimp promotion with stronger financial discipline and limited-time pricing after the permanent offer fueled bankruptcy.
articles.body: Red Lobster is once again offering its Endless Shrimp promotion that contributed to millions of dollars in losses before the seafood chain filed for bankruptcy two years ago. The company told Fox News Digital it decided to bring back Endless Shrimp because the promotion still matters enormously to its customers, who "never stopped asking for it." "They continued telling us they missed it, showed up when we brought it back this spring and kept asking for more after that run ended," Red Lobster said. AMERICA'S CHEAPEST POPCORN SHRIMP BASKET AT A CHAIN RESTAURANT COSTS UNDER $9 "We weren’t going to walk away from something they love simply because the previous operating model did not work," the company added. "The better answer was to fix what didn’t work and bring it back in a way that is right for our guests, our restaurant teams and the company." According to Red Lobster, the spring run also proved the company could bring Endless Shrimp back in a way "that delights our guests and works for our restaurant teams and our business." Participating locations began offering the current Endless Shrimp deal for a limited time Aug. 17. "Guests can mix and match five flavors endlessly throughout the meal for as much shrimp as they like, any way they like it," Red Lobster announced in a press release. The lineup includes new garlic bread-crusted shrimp, shrimp linguini Alfredo, garlic shrimp scampi, Parrot Isle coconut shrimp and Walt’s Favorite Shrimp, hand-breaded, butterflied shrimp lightly fried and served with cocktail sauce. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Red Lobster closed dozens of locations nationwide in May 2024 before filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, Fox News previously reported. Many analysts and media reports have cited the company’s decision to make Endless Shrimp a permanent offering as one factor behind its financial troubles. Endless Shrimp returned to select Red Lobster locations in the spring of 2026, but the chain’s 37-year-old CEO, Damola Adamolekun, made it clear in a statement to affiliate FOX 13 Tampa Bay that the promotion would be available for a limited time only. "The previous model did not work, so we did not repeat it," Red Lobster told Fox News Digital. "We rebuilt Endless Shrimp around much stronger operational and financial discipline, including better forecasting, kitchen flow, menu structure and restaurant support.  "We also designed the current offer to work as a dine-in experience, with pricing that can vary by market. The new standard is simple: Endless Shrimp has to work for the guest, the restaurant team and the business." CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS The spring run of Endless Shrimp "met and exceeded our expectations in several important ways," Red Lobster told Fox News Digital. "Guest satisfaction significantly outperformed the average for Red Lobster promotions, restaurant-team support was stronger than it had been in years and our internal team Proud to Serve and Recommend scores both came in above historical levels," the company said.  "Just as importantly, guests continued asking for Endless Shrimp after the promotion ended." In June 2026, Adamolekun said he was planning "the greatest comeback in the history of the restaurant industry." His plan includes streamlining operations, closing underperforming restaurants, increasing engagement with customers and tapping into their nostalgia. One of the biggest lessons Red Lobster said it learned from the previous Endless Shrimp promotion was that "guest demand alone is not enough." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The changes to Endless Shrimp are one example of how Red Lobster operates differently today, the company said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "We are focused first on the guest, but that guest focus is backed by greater operational discipline and financial rigor. With Endless Shrimp, we took an experience guests love, addressed what wasn’t working and proved we could deliver it successfully under a stronger model. That same approach is guiding the broader business," Red Lobster said.

articles.title: Where water conflicts pose the biggest threat in 2026
articles.summary: Water-related conflicts have nearly quadrupled since 2020. As World Water Week 2026 begins, Al Jazeera unpacks the data.
articles.body:
The sharp rise in water-related conflicts in recent years is in focus as the World Water Week conference begins on Sunday in Sweden’s capital, Stockholm, and online.

With the theme “Water for People and Progress”, the conference is organised annually by the Stockholm International Water Institute (SIWI) and highlights growing global water-security challenges.

According to the Pacific Institute, a US-based nonprofit water think tank, 420 water-related conflicts were recorded in 2024 – a record high and a 78 percent increase from the 235 conflicts recorded in 2022.

The increase is largely driven by attacks on water infrastructure and disputes over access, particularly in regions affected by prolonged wars.

For more than three decades, the Pacific Institute has tracked global water conflicts through its Water Conflict Chronology, classifying each incident by whether water served as a casualty, trigger, or weapon of war.

Casualty: Water infrastructure is damaged or destroyed during conflict, either deliberately or as collateral damage. This can include dams, pipelines, wells, treatment plants and power systems needed to maintain water supplies. In 2024, 55 percent of water-related conflicts were driven by casualty events.

Trigger: Water scarcity, unequal access, or disputes over resources fuel violence, often involving communities, farmers, animal herders, or armed groups. Scarcity and access disputes remain widespread, with 28 percent acting as triggers for water-related conflicts in 2024.

Weapon: Water is deliberately manipulated to harm or pressure opponents, including by cutting supplies, contaminating sources, flooding areas, or controlling access. Water weaponisation is less frequent but persistent, underscoring the growing links between water stress, climate pressures and conflict, with two percent of incidents in 2024 categorised this way.

In Gaza, 1.9 million of 2.1 million people remain displaced, while about 90 percent of water and sanitation infrastructure has been damaged or destroyed by Israeli attacks, according to UNICEF.

Up to 70 percent cannot collect the minimum six litres of water per person a day for drinking and cooking and 90 percent of households faced moderate-to-high water insecurity.

The medical charity, Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF), also known as Doctors Without Borders, reported that water prices have risen by up to 500 percent. Repeated attacks, restrictions on supplies and damage to water facilities have disrupted distribution, worsening diarrhoeal and skin diseases and increasing risks for children and pregnant women, MSF added.

In the occupied West Bank, settler attacks and Israeli demolitions have damaged and destroyed Palestinian water infrastructure, with repeated raids on the Ein Samiya wells east of Ramallah cutting supply to about 100,000 people.

Since April 2023, fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces has displaced about 12 million people and created a humanitarian crisis affecting more than 30 million.

A Geneva Academy report documented attacks on water infrastructure, including reservoirs, treatment plants and distribution networks, particularly in Darfur. The collapse of water and sanitation systems has fuelled cholera outbreaks and worsened food insecurity, with famine risks rising across Darfur, Kordofan and Blue Nile.

US and Israeli air strikes on Iran since February 28, have further strained a water system already weakened by years of drought, below-average rainfall, depleted groundwater and agricultural demand.

Attacks reportedly damaged desalination plants and reservoirs in Qeshm Island and Hormozgan province, disrupting water supplies to tens of thousands of people. Damage to electricity networks and roads has hindered repairs. The attacks came as Iran’s reserves were critically low, with some reservoirs up to 92 percent depleted. Water levels in reservoirs in Mashhad, Iran’s second-largest city and home to around four million people, dropped below three percent.

The war on Iran has exposed the vulnerability of critical water infrastructure in a region that is among the most water-scarce in the world.

Across the Gulf, water security depends heavily on large desalination plants to convert seawater. They supply about 90 percent of drinking water in Kuwait, 86 percent in Oman and 70 percent in Saudi Arabia. In Bahrain, it is above 90 percent and in Qatar, 99 percent.

Desalination plants were damaged in Bahrain, Kuwait, the UAE and Iran during the war, though the reported impact on water supplies was largely limited.

Ukraine’s water crisis has worsened as the war with Russia damages vital water and energy infrastructure. UNICEF says 4.3 million people received safe-water assistance last year, while 12.7 million need humanitarian support.

Attacks have reduced electricity generation by 70 percent, disrupting water and heating. In Kherson, strikes this month cut supplies to entire neighbourhoods.

The Kakhovka Dam disaster in June 2023 affected more than 100,000 people, while about 10 million now lack reliable access to safe water.

articles.title: Nearly three million Teslas recalled in China over hidden door handles
articles.summary: Other brands affected by the recall include Chinese carmakers XPeng, Xiaomi and Geely.
articles.body:
Minimalistic door handles became a signature feature of electric vehicles (EVs), but the controversial designs are now at the centre of China's biggest car recall, affecting more than 4 million vehicles.

The recall, which includes 2.98 million Chinese-made Teslas, follows safety concerns that the hidden door handles are difficult to locate and open in emergency situations.

Other brands affected by the recall include Chinese carmakers XPeng, Xiaomi and Geely.

The recalled vehicles will have a warning label stuck on the interior door and receive a software update to automatically lower the windows in a crash.

The designs have come under scrutiny after two fatal crashes in China involving Xiaomi EVs, in which power failures were suspected to have prevented doors from being opened.

Tesla said in a statement on Friday that it was recalling some of its Model 3, Y, S and X vehicles due to door handles that are "difficult to identify and operate because their colour is similar to the interior trim".

"In extreme situations such as a severe collision causing the vehicle's low-voltage system to fail, this could hinder occupants from quickly opening the doors to escape and impede rescue efforts by those outside the vehicle, posing a safety hazard," it said.

Tesla said it would place warning labels on the recalled vehicles and issue a software update to automatically lower a vehicle's windows after a collision.

The BBC understands that carmakers have not yet notified authorities of any plans for a similar recall in the US.

The BBC has contacted Tesla, XPeng, Xiaomi and Geely for comment.

The use of hidden handle designs has "snowballed" after Chinese brands were quick to copy the "sleek" look of Tesla's Model S sedan since 2014, said Tu Le, the managing director of consultancy Sino Auto Insights.

The use of warning labels and a software update is more of a "band-aid" than a lasting solution for the issue, he added.

In February, Chinese authorities announced a ban on hidden door handles .

Under new rules due to take effect on 1 January 2027, cars will only be allowed to be sold in China if they have a mechanical release on both the inside and outside of their doors.

Tesla's door handles were also involved in a probe by US safety regulators after reports that they suddenly stopped working, leaving children trapped in the cars.

In July, the US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration suggested creating a new formal safety standard for all carmakers.

The agency told the BBC that it is reviewing whether it will require emergency door-exit systems in vehicles.

The world's carmakers are struggling to compete with China

Tesla cuts car models in shift to robots and AI

articles.summary: Middle East News: At least two people, including a four-year-old boy, were killed and seven others wounded in two Israeli airstrikes in the Gaza Strip on Sunday.This co.
articles.body: At least two people, including a four-year-old boy, were killed and seven others wounded in two Israeli airstrikes in the Gaza Strip on Sunday.This comes as Israel threatened to intensify attacks following what it said were launches of balloons, drones and kites from Gaza towards Israel.One of the strikes hit a building in the central town of Zawayda after the Israeli army warned the propertyâs owners to evacuate, residents said.Medics said flying debris and shrapnel scattered over an area spanning dozens of metres, injuring at least six people, including four-year-old Mohammad Abdel-Salam Taha, who was later pronounced dead at a hospital.âThere is no ceasefire, there is nothing,â said Abu Ahmed, a displaced Palestinian sheltering near the building, which the airstrike reduced to a pile of mangled steel and concrete."We want solutions, we want to live âin peace," he added, as cited by Reuters.The second airstrike struck the nearby Nuseirat refugee camp, Palestinian health officials said.The strikes came as Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned that Israel would intensify targeted attacks against those responsible for launching drones, balloons and kites from the Gaza Strip if the launches did not stop immediately.Hamas, meanwhile, accused Israel of using children's kites as a pretext to escalate "attacks" on Gaza.In a post on X, the prime minister of Israel's official account said Netanyahu and defence minister Israel Katz held "a situational assessment this evening regarding the threat of drones, balloons and kites launched from the Gaza Strip toward Israel."The meeting was attended by Chief of the General Staff Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, the Head of the National Security Council and senior IDF officials.Israel issued a warning against Hamas that "if the launches toward Israel do not cease immediately, the IDF will act to increase targeted strikes against those responsible for the launches and will evacuate the population from areas used as launch sites for kites, drones, and balloons."The developments came as US special envoy Jared Kushner said Washington had made significant progress during a nearly four-hour meeting with Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu on August 17.The discussions focused on Gazaâs reconstruction, demilitarisation and Israelâs security concerns.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: âCTA intentionally preventedâ: PTI alleges negligence over Imran Khanâs hospital visit
articles.summary: Pakistan News: Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), the party of former Prime Minister Imran Khan, on Monday criticised what it called the âcontinued failureâ of authorit.
articles.body: Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), the party of former Prime Minister Imran Khan, on Monday criticised what it called the âcontinued failureâ of authorities at a state-run hospital, alleging that a CT Coronary Angiography (CTA) scheduled for Khan was not conducted despite cardiologists warning of potential cardiac complications.In a statement on Sunday, PTI central secretary Information Sheikh Waqas Akram said authorities had failed to provide the 73-year-old Khan with the medically recommended diagnostic test despite a functional CT scanner being available at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS), Dawn reported."This cannot be dismissed as an isolated administrative lapse; it reflects a deeply troubling pattern,â Akram said.Akram also cited a Supreme Court order directing Khan to undergo a comprehensive medical examination and treatment at Shifa International Hospital.He alleged that authorities had bypassed the directive and instead transferred Khan to a facility where the CT angiography was not conducted.âWhen the necessary facilities were available at Shifa International, deliberately taking Khan to a hospital unable or unwilling to perform the procedure raises a grave question: was the decision made in advance to prevent the CT Coronary Angiography from being conducted?â he asked."Even the governmentâs own doctors considered this diagnostic test necessary,â Akram added.Akram said a government medical board examined Khan on August 10 after he complained of heart palpitations and severe headaches.He said a cardiologist at PIMS had recommended a CTA on August 1 after Khan experienced fluctuating blood pressure and restlessness, citing potential cardiac complications given his age and prolonged isolation.Taking note of the reports, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Saturday formed an inquiry committee, headed by the Establishment Division secretary, to establish the facts and determine responsibility.Commenting on the Prime Ministerâs decision to constitute an inquiry committee following reports that Imran Khanâs CTA was not conducted, Akram said the move raised âserious questions as to why the medically recommended test was not conducted in the first instance. Why coordination between the cardiology and radiology departments had failed, and why Imran Khan was not taken to Shifa International despite the availability of the required facilities thereâ."Imran Khanâs heart health cannot be subjected to political calculations, administrative excuses or further delay,â Akram said."Political victimisation must never be permitted to endanger a human life through the denial or postponement of essential medical care. The decision to take him to a facility where the required test was not conducted, despite the availability of the necessary facilities at Shifa International, has created serious concerns that the procedure was intentionally prevented,â he alleged."The government and all relevant authorities will bear full responsibility for any further deterioration in his condition,â Akram added.Meanwhile, former India captains Sunil Gavaskar, Kapil Dev and Dilip Vengsarkar are among 21 former international cricket captains who have written to Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, urging authorities to ensure proper medical treatment and the welfare of Imran Khan.The letter, initiated by former Australia captain Greg Chappell, marks the second appeal by former international cricketers calling for humane treatment and adequate medical care for the 73-year-old Khan.Khan was arrested on August 5, 2023, in connection with a corruption case and has remained in custody since then. He is currently lodged in Adiala Jail, a detention facility on the outskirts of Rawalpindi.Khanâs relatives and supporters have repeatedly alleged human rights violations and accused authorities of restricting his access to adequate medical care, family visits and legal counsel.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Ancient clue cracks open a 2,000-year-old mystery near famed Colosseum
articles.summary: Archaeologists working near Rome's Colosseum uncovered eight rooms with mosaics and painted decorations that may belong to an ancient Roman firehouse.
articles.body: Archaeologists digging near Rome's Colosseum believe they may have found an ancient firehouse dating back nearly 2,000 years. The building, which dates to the second century A.D., was found in the Villa Celimontana park near the Colosseum, Reuters reported this month. Villa Celimontana dates to the 16th century, when it was developed as a noble residence on Caelian Hill, one of the seven hills of ancient Rome. CONSTRUCTION WORKERS CLEARING OLD BOMBS UNEXPECTEDLY FIND 'IMPORTANT' ANCIENT SANCTUARY The discovery was originally announced by Rome's archaeological superintendency, part of Italy's Ministry of Culture. At the excavation site, archaeologists fully uncovered five of the building's eight rooms, which contain mosaics and remnants of painted decorations. Officials believe the building may have been part of the nearby barracks of the Fifth Cohort of the Vigiles, ancient Rome's firefighting force. They cited one telling clue: A mosaic found at the site closely resembles one previously discovered in a firefighters' barracks in Ostia, ancient Rome's port city. ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER SPRAWLING ROMAN ESTATE BURIED FOR CENTURIES BENEATH FARMLAND The Vigiles were also tasked with maintaining public order at night, and their nearby barracks used water from an aqueduct. "If this hypothesis is confirmed, the discovery would help reassess the extent of one of the most important military complexes of imperial Rome," officials said in a statement. Pictures show the remains of the ancient building, including exposed walls and sections uncovered during the excavation. Other images show fragments of mosaic uncovered at the site. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Another possibility, said officials, is that the structure was a private residence, or domus, similar to others found on Caelian Hill. The elaborate decorations could support that hypothesis, officials said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "Only a thorough study of the excavation materials and the structures exposed will provide further information on the newly discovered structure," the superintendency said. The possible firehouse is the latest in a string of ancient Roman discoveries to emerge across Italy in recent months. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Archaeologists recently uncovered an ancient city along Italy's famed Appian Way, complete with a forum and theater and dating back more than 2,000 years. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Earlier this summer, officials announced another major archaeological discovery near the Colosseum — the remains of an ancient Roman villa found beneath a high school gym. Reuters contributed reporting.

articles.title: The Rockefellers Have Moved the Same Fortune Through Six Generations Without a Single Estate-Tax Bill. The 1934 Trusts They Used Are Still Legal, and Still for Sale.
articles.summary: The Rockefeller family has passed the same fortune through six generations without triggering a single federal estate tax bill, and the legal structure they...
articles.body:
Dynasty trusts remove assets from a taxable estate permanently, letting wealth compound across generations without triggering a 40% estate tax at each death.

The $15 million federal exemption, made permanent in 2026, defines who benefits. Estates comfortably below that threshold gain nothing from this structure.

Forgetting to allocate GST exemption on IRS Form 709 in the gift year exposes every future generational transfer to a flat 40% tax.

If you have real wealth and a taxable estate on the horizon, the Rockefeller family structure offers a template. In 1934, John D. Rockefeller Jr. locked most of the family fortune into a set of irrevocable trusts that have since carried assets through six generations without a single federal estate tax bill. The structure has a name: Dynasty Trust, and it is still legal in 2026.

A dynasty trust is an irrevocable trust designed to hold assets for as long as state law allows, sometimes forever. Once funded, the assets leave the grantor's taxable estate. They grow inside the trust. When the children die, then the grandchildren, then the great-grandchildren, the trust keeps going, and the IRS does not get a fresh 40% estate tax bite at each death. That mechanism turned the 1934 Rockefeller trusts into a six-generation compounding vehicle.

The trust can own almost anything: public stock, private company shares, real estate, life insurance, a family business. Distributions go to beneficiaries under rules written into the document. Everything the trust does not distribute keeps compounding outside the transfer-tax system.

If you've saved over $1,000,000, this guide is for you. The last thing you want in retirement is to run out of money, you want your money to generate lasting income while you enjoy your life.

Now you can learn the strategies wealthy retirees use to fund their retirement with The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income from Fisher Investments. Download the guide today! (sponsor)

Two federal laws make this whole arrangement possible. The estate and gift tax rules are found in Subtitle B of the Internal Revenue Code, with sections 2001 through 2058 covering the estate tax and sections 2501 through 2524 covering the gift tax. Then there is the generation-skipping transfer tax, or GST tax, which Congress added in 1976 specifically to close the dynasty-trust loophole, and that lives in IRC sections 2601 through 2664. The GST tax hits at a flat 40% on any transfers that skip a generation. The real key that makes a dynasty trust work today is IRC section 2631, which grants every individual a GST exemption that can be allocated to a trust so future distributions never trigger that tax.

articles.title: Washington Post ordered to reinstate columnist Karen Attiah after being terminated over Charlie Kirk posts
articles.summary: The Washington Post has been ordered to reinstate columnist Karen Attiah after being fired for Bluesky posts about Charlie Kirk's assassination.
articles.body: The Washington Post was ordered to reinstate columnist Karen Attiah after she was fired last year for social media posts she made after Charlie Kirk's assassination. Sarah Miller Espinosa, the arbitrator overseeing Attiah's legal challenge against The Post, said the paper "did not have good and sufficient cause" and that it "violated" her labor agreement, according to The New York Times, which first reported on Espinosa's ruling last Thursday. "The Washington Post failed to establish the grievant engaged in gross misconduct," Espinosa concluded. TEACHERS WHO CELEBRATED CHARLIE KIRK'S ASSASSINATION NOW CASH IN WITH TAXPAYER-FUNDED SETTLEMENTS Attiah told The Times she is "relieved to finally have that record set straight," adding, "This decision confirms what we’ve said from the start: I was doing my job as an opinion writer, and this was wrongful termination." The columnist announced her legal victory, saying on X, "The Washington Post fired me last year for speaking the truth after Charlie Kirk's killing. I fought back. I'm happy to announce: I won my case against the Washington Post. They have been ordered to reinstate me immediately." "In general, if someone reveals themselves to be a ghoul then companies should be able to fire them," Turning Point USA spokesman Andrew Kolvet told Fox News Digital.  A spokesperson for The Washington Post said the paper respects the arbitration process and declined to comment further. Attiah didn't immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Attiah sparked outrage for her posts about the slain conservative icon on the liberal social media platform Bluesky. TENNESSEE UNIVERSITY TO PAY PROFESSOR $1.9M AFTER CALLING CHARLIE KIRK A 'DISGUSTING PSYCHOPATH' GEORGIA TEACHER RECEIVES ALMOST $300K SETTLEMENT OVER CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSINATION POST "Refusing to tear my clothes and smear ashes on my face in performative mourning for a White man that espoused violence is… not the same as violence," Attiah wrote at the time. In a separate post, she wrote, "Part of what keeps America so violent is the insistence that people perform care, empty goodness and absolution for White men who espouse hatred and violence.’" Critics also slammed Attiah for misquoting Kirk in another post, attributing to him saying, "Black women do not have the brain processing power to be taken seriously. You have to go steal a White person's slot." On a July 2023 episode of "The Charlie Kirk Show," Kirk actually said, "If we would have said three weeks ago [...] that Joy Reid and Michelle Obama, and Sheila Jackson Lee, and Ketanji Brown Jackson were affirmative-action picks, we would have been called racist. But now they're comin' out and they're saying it for us! They're comin' out, and they're saying, 'I'm only here because of affirmative action.' Yeah, we know. You do not have the brain processing power to otherwise be taken really seriously. You had to go steal a White person's slot to go be taken somewhat seriously." Following the backlash, Attiah revealed she had been fired by The Post, saying in a termination letter her posts were "unacceptable" and "gross misconduct." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Attiah filed a legal challenge against The Post over her termination last fall, and previously announced in June that she and the paper would enter arbitration.
