articles.title: Terror threat looms over coastal destination as US warns attacks could strike without notice
articles.summary: Terrorists have targeted upscale lodges where international big-game hunters stay in Mozambique's Cabo Delgado Province, the State Department warns.
articles.body: Americans are being warned to avoid parts of an African safari destination where terrorists have targeted upscale lodges frequented by international big-game hunters. Mozambique, a southeastern African country across from the island of Madagascar, is the subject of an Aug. 21 updated "Level 2: Exercise Increased Caution" advisory from the U.S. State Department. Officials have also designated multiple areas "Level 4: Do Not Travel" — citing heightened terrorism risks. AMERICANS WARNED POPULAR TRAVEL ROUTES THIS SUMMER COULD CARRY CRIME AND KIDNAPPING RISKS Bordered by Tanzania, Malawi, Zambia, Zimbabwe, South Africa and Eswatini, Mozambique is known for its Indian Ocean coastline, beaches and wildlife reserves. Though not a tourist hot spot, Mozambique draws visitors for its safari tourism. It welcomed over 757,400 foreign guests in 2024, according to government statistics. Cabo Delgado Province, a "Do Not Travel" area, is home to safari and wildlife destinations, including Quirimbas National Park. The State Department also warns that terrorist groups in northern Mozambique are "active" and that there is a risk of terrorist violence and attacks. ROBBERIES, ASSAULTS AND RAPES SPUR NEW US TRAVEL WARNING FOR POPULAR CARIBBEAN GETAWAY "Attackers may strike public areas and tourist destinations with little or no warning, sometimes taking hostages," the advisory says. Alex Perry, an England-based author and veteran foreign correspondent who previously served as a TIME bureau chief, told Fox News Digital the terrorist presence in northern Mozambique is relatively small but particularly brutal. "Mozambique has one of the smaller ISIS groups in the world," Perry said, estimating it has roughly 500 members. "They are spectacularly nasty." Perry, author of the book "Blood Will Flow" about the deadly Islamist insurgency in Mozambique, said militants in Cabo Delgado have carried out mass beheadings, and that the region's tourism industry has suffered as a result of the insurgency. Cabo Delgado has historically attracted a more exclusive clientele, with smaller numbers of wealthy visitors paying high prices for hunting safaris compared with Africa's major mass-market safari destinations, he also said. "They are spectacularly nasty." "This is almost exclusively hunting safaris — people going to shoot animals," Perry said. "That tends to be much smaller numbers of people paying a much higher price." The State Department says Americans who opt to travel to Mozambique are encouraged to enroll in the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP). CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Those who must travel to affected areas of Cabo Delgado, Niassa and Nampula provinces are also advised to consider hiring a security firm. "Avoid all but emergency travel between sunset and sunrise," the advisory says, adding that Americans should "keep a low profile." "Have evacuation plans that do not rely on U.S. government assistance. Have travel documents up to date and easily accessible." CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Perry said that, although the advisory highlights serious risks, much of Mozambique remains a beautiful destination for travelers. "On the whole, it's a pretty safe and secure and, as I say, beautiful and enjoyable place to visit," Perry said. "The far north is a dramatic exception." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Fox News Digital reached out to the U.S. State Department for further insights. The warning is one of several travel advisories issued or updated by the State Department in recent months, as officials continue flagging safety concerns for Americans traveling abroad. This month, the State Department issued a Level 2 travel advisory for Ecuador, warning Americans to exercise increased caution due to violent crime, terrorism and kidnapping. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Earlier this summer, the U.S. renewed a Level 2 "Exercise Increased Caution" advisory for the Bahamas.

articles.title: Charity? Acting? The Cotswolds? What will Harry and Meghan's UK life look like?
articles.summary: The couple's return to the UK is imminent - and what they'll be focusing on here is gradually becoming clearer.
articles.body:
Within the next few days, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex and their two children will have departed California and become residents of the UK.

Since news broke of the move, there has been some confusion as to what British life for Harry and Meghan will look like - but a picture is emerging of the family's priorities.

Over the weekend, there was a deluge of stories about Meghan's return to acting with speculation she would have a role in the next series of The Gentlemen on Netflix, created by British director Guy Ritchie.

Talks are still said to be in the early stages and we understand filming for the third series of the show is imminent - but Netflix has made no comment on who will star, leaving the way open for a former working member of the royal family with an acting background to be cast.

The comedy is about a duke turned drug baron and is mostly filmed in the Cotswolds.

What is clear is that a return to acting more broadly is very much on the agenda for Meghan. It would be financially lucrative for the family in a world of expensive homes, school fees and international travel.

Speaking in June last year to British businesswoman and podcaster Emma Grede, Meghan talked about her Netflix lifestyle series With Love, Meghan, and hinted at a return to acting when asked if she missed that side to her life.

"Sometimes," Meghan replied. "Being back on set with With Love, Meghan was great because I realised how much I miss my crew. I love being around a crew."

But Variety's chief correspondent Marlow Stern says when it comes to deliberations over a potential acting role for Meghan, "a lot of it has to do with scheduling, to be honest".

"They're maybe also negotiating the size of the role and how many days she'll shoot, and also compensation for it. Both sides often play the media to try and push things along, and we could be seeing that."

For Harry, the focus once back in the UK will be on the charity work and patronages he has kept hold of while living thousands of miles away.

He has now completed his final charity engagements in the US before flying back to the UK in the coming days.

In Washington DC, he met military veterans and their families and visited America's main hospital for injured servicemen and women, Walter Reed National Military Medical Centre.

At Arlington National Cemetery, he visited the final resting place of many service personal killed in Iraq and Afghanistan wars where he himself served on two operational tours.

At the grave of Sergeant Michael Verardo, who died last year from complications related to injuries sustained in Afghanistan in 2010, he met Verardo's widow Sarah - who now supports other military families - and their nine-year-old daughter, Elizabeth.

"All my daughter knows about princes or princesses is probably contained to a movie... she whispered to me and said, 'Where is his crown? Did he leave it in the car?'" Sarah said.

"She was very dazzled by the ability to meet him and it made us find bits of sparkle for her at a young age in a very hard experience - and that means a lot to me personally."

It is a reminder of the impact Prince Harry is able to make and what he will hope to bring to an increased amount of public work in the UK.

Plans for a number of charity engagements in September in Britain were already in place.

He will be at the WellChild Awards in London towards the end of the month, continuing his support for the event which honours the bravery of seriously ill children.

There will inevitably be an emphasis on the Invictus Games for wounded service personnel which will be held in Birmingham next July.

In an ideal world, the King, as head of the Armed Forces, would officially open the Games - putting father and son together in public for the first time in several years.

That remains an aspiration from Invictus organisers rather than any definitive plan.

Based in the Cotswolds, settling into school

It's thought the family will base themselves in the Cotswolds. Harry and Meghan previously rented a property there in 2018 and are known to have friends in the area.

Reports that the couple have turned to former Spice Girl Geri Horner and her husband Christian Horner for advice on life in the area have been rejected by Harry and Meghan's official spokesperson.

"Harry and Meghan are great fans of Geri and Christian… the Horners are not advising them on their return, nor have they been asked to do so."

The couple will be back in the UK about a week before the autumn school term begins for their two children, seven-year-old Archie and five-year-old Lilibet. Most terms begin at the end of next week.

It's understood Meghan will concentrate on settling her children into the routine of life in a British school. She is not expected to embark on any kind of full programme of public engagements.

Exploring acting opportunities and running her business, As Ever, will fill her time once her family is settled. She may also appear alongside her husband at some of his charity events.

The couple will keep their multi-million dollar home in Montecito, about a two-hour drive north of Los Angeles. Meghan's mother, Doria Ragland, who has been heavily involved in helping to care for her grandchildren, will remain living in California.

The family is expected to return to the US regularly as well as use the holiday home they have bought near Melides in Portugal.

It is close to a property bought by Princess Eugenie and her husband Jack Brooksbank who have remained close to the Sussexes during the royal fallout.

How involved Harry, Meghan, Archie and Lilibet will be with the wider royal family has not yet been decided.

Over the next few months, several significant royal engagements are in the diary that would involve most senior royals - Remembrance Sunday at the Cenotaph, the Princess of Wales' Carol Service at Westminster Abbey and then Christmas at Sandringham.

Will there be invitations extended to the Sussex family?

Trust remains an issue. There is caution, a degree of wariness and even hostility in some quarters of the Royal Household. These decisions are very much a work in progress.

Harry and Meghan's team has described the move to the UK as being for "an extended period of time".

It is not necessarily a long-term move but may be a chance for the family to experience life in the UK, allowing the children to get to know their grandfather, the King, while they are young enough to not have their education disrupted.

Much of what happens in the months ahead will be a test - of Harry and Meghan's liking for life in the UK, of public reaction to them and of the royal family's ability to continue with their duties alongside the distractions the Sussex family may bring.

As they return to the UK, Harry and Meghan search for a brand that sticks

What happened to Harry and Meghan's American dream?

Harry and Meghan's team has described the move to the UK as being for "an extended period of time".

It is not necessarily a long-term move but may be a chance for the family to experience life in the UK, allowing the children to get to know their grandfather, the King, while they are young enough to not have their education disrupted.

Much of what happens in the months ahead will be a test - of Harry and Meghan's liking for life in the UK, of public reaction to them and of the royal family's ability to continue with their duties alongside the distractions the Sussex family may bring.

articles.title: China's humanoid robots are stealing the show, but a quieter machine revolution is unfolding
articles.summary: There are more than two million robots working in China's factories - and they are scaling up fast.
articles.body:
"I take a nap and the world changes," says Chen Tianyu.

His world certainly does. The 28-year-old keeps up with the latest technology by spending his spare time in factories that are switching to automation. That way he knows what to prioritise when teaching his class about artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics.

In front of him, around 30 college students are studying code. One of them is typing furiously as his eyes dart from the screen to the robot: "The idea is it will grab that cylindrical piece and move it over there."

A line of industrial robots are waiting to be programmed, and in another part of the classroom, students are trying to develop robotic medical instruments. As he guides them, Chen declares: "If you are not needed by the world of AI and robotics, then you'll definitely be among those eliminated".

For the people in this room, this is a step - or rather a leap - towards a future that China is meticulously building: Xi Jinping's $20bn (£14.7bn) plan to put his country at the forefront of innovation and in direct competition with the US.

The evidence is all around them. They are in the Hangzhou Technician Institute, one of several huge, purpose-built vocational schools that want to churn out the next generation of tech-savvy engineers. The campus sits on the outskirts of Hangzhou, a former imperial capital whose futuristic skyline is just the first hint of its role as a global tech hub.

Across the country, there are more than two million robots working in China's factories - which is more than anywhere else - and they are continuing to scale up at extraordinary speed.

It is a commitment that will surely change the world, much like the last time the Chinese economy underwent a massive transformation. It is already shipping its robots across the globe: more than half of the world's industrial robots are now made in China.

What is less clear is the impact of such sweeping automation in a country that sits at the heart of global manufacturing, trade and innovation. What does this mean for China's human workforce, for instance? And how would we be able to truly measure the cost of this transformation in a regime that controls information so tightly?

The future of China's workers is uncertain in the industrial revolution the world has been watching: gleaming solar grids, peak hours made noiseless by electric vehicles, machines that run faster than Usain Bolt. Over the weekend, China hosted the second edition of the World Humanoid Games where robots boxed, sprinted and marched.

What is fuelling this spectacle is another, less visible revolution happening inside factories and classrooms.

The BBC has visited industrial sites where we have been shown robots that do not look human, or dance or leap on stage but weld, paint, lift, assemble and work around the clock without a break or benefits. Some are designed to build more robots. We have also been inside academies where China is training the people who will work alongside its robotic workforce.

This is a front-row seat to what Xi calls China's "new productive forces" - and how they could reshape the country.

On a factory floor in the southern city of Chengdu, the old and and the new are working side by side.

An assembly line of around 30 middle-aged men and women is screwing, drilling and polishing CRP Technology's signature product: a robotic arm which performs various industrial tasks. Also in the room are four young engineers crowded around a console, trying to crack the code for a prototype, a new robot that they hope will help build other robots.

One of them, 31-year-old Pang Kai, who is part of the research and development team, pushes the sleek skeleton across the room. Because China's future workforce is not quite ready to strut out. For now, it can only do simple repetitive movements, such as scan a QR code.

"Maybe in another half year, it can do another task," Pang says, smiling wistfully. It's a long road and the team are celebrating every small win.

CRP Technology, which employs around 300 people, has been building robot arms for nine years. Each arm can be tailored to a factory's needs to help build cars, electronics or wind turbines. The firm says a single arm can be programmed to perform more than 90% of repetitive tasks.

The engineers also wonder if, one day, they can replace the company's workforce. "We want our new robot to be like human beings. We hope it can think by itself," says Pang. "We need these kinds of robots because maybe in 10 years, we won't have enough workers in China."

A shrinking population and an ageing workforce is another reason Beijing is in a hurry to revolutionise its factories. By 2035, more than a third of China's population will be over 60, according to official estimates. The country will also lose nearly 60 million people in the next decade - almost equivalent to the population of France - according to some estimates.

The hope is that increased automation will fill this looming gap in the workforce before it starts to affect an already sluggish economy. But the speed of the transition is key. Around 120 million people still work in the manufacturing sector. If China moves too quickly, job losses could follow dealing a catastrophic blow to millions who depend on factory wages.

"In theory, machines can work 24 hours a day, which is certainly an advantage compared with human workers. But machines also require maintenance. Every day we need time for that, and each month the production line also requires inspection and repair," says Cao Li, vice-president of EV maker Leapmotor.

Increasingly popular in Europe and the UK, the company's budget-friendly, tech-focused cars come together at the Hangzhou factory with robots aiding the process at every step. At the end of the assembly line, more humans emerge.

The company has more than 25,000 workers and hundreds of them make the final checks as the sparkling new vehicles roll past. Will there be a day when they are no longer needed?

"It's entirely possible," Cao says. "And it may come relatively quickly. In workshops, including stamping, welding, and painting, we've basically achieved 100% automation."

China has the edge over the US due to its enormous manufacturing base. Motors, batteries, electronics, gears, sensors - everything needed to build the body of a robot is all at hand.

"China also has an idea. It has a plan. They know where they want to be in five years. They plan at a top level, but they break it down to the regions, to the municipalities," says Dr Susanne Bieller, General Secretary of the International Federation of Robotics.

"If you want to build a robot in Shenzhen - there's an entire ecosystem. It takes you less than one hour to source the components you need to make a robot. In Europe it can take you up to a week."

However, she acknowledges that while China is good at building the body, the US is still leading at building the "brain", which includes developing the AI to programme robots. And yet Chinese firms, from DeepSeek to Moonshot, have been unveiling new AI models that they say can compete with top US firms.

Driven by an "open-source" approach, where AI start-ups share their code, Chinese innovation has been able to catch up faster than expected, despite US export controls over critical advanced chips. Analysts now believe that the next leg of this race will be determined not by who has the best language model, but who can put this intelligence into millions of machines.

And that is why China is also investing in producing a generation of students learning to imagine what could come next.

At the Hangzhou Technician Institute, for example, children can start from the age of 15. And the scale of what is being taught can feel staggering. There is an entire building dedicated to engines and aeronautics, and a restricted floor for students who will work to keep China at the forefront of processing rare earths - another crucial commodity in the battle with Washington.

Some see this as a solution to China's stubbornly high youth unemployment rate, with one in five struggling to find a job. "Our students are in demand and can even be pre-booked by companies. They don't need to worry about employment at all, and we hold competitions as part of their training," Chen, the young teacher, says.

"It's better to find your position within the technological wave. In the process of progress, structural changes are bound to occur, and these structural changes are exactly where students' future employment opportunities lie."

But China still faces serious economic challenges, from a property crisis that continues to drag on to huge local government debt and persistently low consumption.

It is unclear if and how the revolution Beijing is touting will fix these, and it is hard to gauge how those whose jobs are threatened feel about the change that is coming. Will robots create prosperity for them, or simply take many of their jobs?

"My students ask me what will happen in the future," Chen says. "I say I don't know. Technology is changing so fast. But we can't just stand still and sleep here. We have to move forward to see what we are capable of doing."

A decade on, Trump returns to a stronger and more assertive China

articles.title: AI flooding public bodies with complaints and requests
articles.body:
A rising tide of complaints written with the help of AI is substantially increasing the workload of schools, local councils and other public bodies, the BBC has been told.

Chatbots can produce complex arguments, often quoting regulations or acts of Parliament, with documents running to dozens of pages long.

One body said complaints once contained to a single sheet of A4 could now run to 20 pages. They said AI also made errors and sometimes misquoted legislation, and further added to the time it takes to deal with grievances.

Many people say AI makes complaining more accessible and effective, with one person telling the BBC it has "made a real practical difference in how I've been able to represent myself".

However, Deborah Evans, chief executive of Lawyers in Local Government - which represents 5,600 lawyers working in local authorities - estimated her organisation needed double the current workforce to deal with the "massive" increase in complaints.

Dawn Harverson, who struggles with writing, said AI can help people complain more easily.

"In the past, you'd be able to pick up the phone and speak to somebody," she told the BBC.

"We're all pushed down this road to send emails, and so somebody who's neurodivergent or intimidated by the written word will just simply not complain."

Posts across social media also testify to the popularity of using AI to challenge parking fines or appeal benefits decisions.

Evans said she welcomed the fact that AI was helping more people exercise their right to complain.

However, she said it had "increased the number of trivial or unjustified complaints", along with their complexity.

Without AI, she said, a complaint might be "one side of A4 about your bins not being emptied".

"But when AI gets involved, the complexity and length of that complaint ramps up enormously," she said. "A complaint could be between 19 and 27 pages, include case law, and quote various Acts of Parliament."

Complaints handlers might then need to consult lawyers, adding to councils' costs.

To meet this rising workload by increasing staff alone "you'd be doubling your workforce on complaint handling", she said.

In practice, it would most likely result in slower responses, she added.

What is AI, how does it work and why are some people concerned about it?

Evans said councils needed to consider alternative solutions, such as using forms to limit the length of complaints.

But some regard such measures as a way to curtail accountability.

The Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman Amerdeep Clarke - which investigates individual complaints about councils - told the BBC AI needed to be used with "discretion".

"We have also seen a rise in the use of AI in legal challenges to our decisions," she added.

School leaders have also reported a rise in complex cases linked to AI.

Pepe Di'Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, told the BBC complaints were rising for a variety of reasons and AI was adding to the effort needed to deal with them.

"Often schools also see parents using AI to generate multiple and extensive complaints which adds to the difficulty in resolving these issues and puts further strain on staff," he said.

Public sector workers told the BBC they support the use of AI as a way remove barriers to challenging decisions.

But the difficulty is in how to preserve that while discouraging time-wasting requests.

AI is increasingly used to help request data from public authorities under the UK's Freedom of Information (FOI) Act.

People can complain to the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) when they believe information has been wrongly withheld, or they haven't had a response in time.

The ICO said in May it had been told FOI teams were seeing "higher volumes of requests, a greater complexity of request" - including some which "misquote legislation or require significant clarification before they can be processed".

The UK's data watchdog even published guidance on the issue , saying: "Without clear, practical support, this trend risks placing pressure on FOI teams and could lead to delays, errors or increased complaints."

Lynn Wyeth, a digital officer at the National Association of Data Protection Officers - a membership body for those handling FOIs - said AI-assisted requests appeared to be "creating a hidden workload".

"They frequently lead to longer correspondence, clarification exercises and long complex appeals," she said.

She said public authorities needed the go-ahead to use AI themselves in order to deal with the increase in requests.

Harverson says AI, like any tool, needs to be used thoughtfully.

"If people are just going to press send on a very elaborate email complaint, then OK that might be taking up time, but then that's just a bad use of AI," she said.

BBC Radio 5 Live was also contacted by listeners who had seen increases in the length and number of complaints written by AI in their jobs.

One said it was clear that more and more complaints they were receiving were AI produced, and often quoted incorrect legislation

However another listener, who said they worked for a global company, said they used AI to reduce "50+ page" AI-generated complaints into a one-page response which "has proven very effective in closing things down".

Another, who worked on a voluntary basis as a school governor, said the fact that AI chatbots are often programmed to agree with the user meant they did not push back.

"AI doesn't turn around to the complainant and say, actually I don't think this is worth it," they wrote.

But a primary school teacher said AI helps parents who struggle to put their complaints into writing - and suggested the "old-fashioned" way of speaking to them face-to-face to resolve issues.

They wrote: "Maybe the issue isn't the use of AI, but the inability to talk to human beings in public services these days?"

OpenAI makes ChatGPT less 'human' for teens in new safety update

OpenAI says its AI went rogue and launched 'unprecedented' cyber-attack

Microsoft boss troubled by rise in reports of 'AI psychosis'

articles.title: In 1999, the Azores protected forest for the endangered Azores bullfinch; two decades of restoration later, surveys estimated about 1,300 birds in suitable habitat
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover how dedicated conservation efforts have helped restore the Azores bullfinch population from 100 pairs in 1999 to over 1,300 individuals today by revitalizing their habitat in the Azores.
articles.body: In 1999, the Azores set aside the Pico da Vara/Ribeira do Guilherme region on SÃ£o Miguel Island for the conservation of the endangered Azores bullfinch, a bird found nowhere else in the world. At the time, the bird species had been reduced to around 100 breeding pairs and survived in a small remnant of native laurel forest. More than two decades later, sustained habitat restoration transformed about 1,000 acres of its core habitat, and surveys estimated the bird population at around 1,300 individuals. The Smithsonian notes that this recovery followed years of removing invasive plants, restoring native forests, and planting more than 500,000 native trees.A species confined to a shrinking forestThe Azores bullfinch, locally known as the Priolo and scientifically as Pyrrhula murina, is endemic to SÃ£o Miguel, the biggest island in the Azores archipelago, and its decline followed centuries of changes to the islandâs native vegetation. A 2011 study published in Bird Conservation International evaluated annual monitoring data from 1991 to 2008, confirming that the historical population decline had successfully halted and stabilised shortly after the 1999 conservation measures were enacted. Instead of a continuing downward spiral, this tracking window proved that protecting the remaining laurel forest on the eastern side of the island provided an immediate, vital lifeline against habitat degradation.The birdâs dependence on native vegetation made habitat restoration central to its survival. Jamie Ramosâ research, which was later published in Biological Conservation, helped establish the importance of the bullfinchâs diet and habitat preferences. The study showed that the species feeds on a range of native plants and their seeds, buds and other parts, meaning that replacing native forest with invasive vegetation could reduce both available habitat and food. Ramosâ work reportedly helped conservationists conclude that protecting and expanding native forest was more important than simply trying to manage the bird directly.Notably, the conservation situation was serious enough that the International Union for Conservation of Nature listed the Azores bullfinch as Critically Endangered in 2005. However, the formal protection of its core habitat had already begun by then, with the Pico da Vara/Ribeira do Guilherme area designated for bird conservation in 1999. This milestone established the legal framework necessary to secure international funding over the next four years.The process of removing invasive plants and rebuilding native forestFollowing the administrative steps, major restoration work began in 2003, when the Portuguese Society for the Study of Birds (SPEA), working with the Azores government and European Union LIFE funding, began a dedicated conservation programme. Smithsonian reported that the first five-year project concentrated on improving forest quality by planting native trees. Later LIFE projects expanded the work, including establishing a nursery capable of producing a large number of native plants.Conservationists had to remove the invasive vegetation that had displaced the native plants. Managed in sequence, the LIFE Priolo project ran from 2003 to 2008, followed immediately by the LIFE Sustainable Laurel Forest project from 2009 to 2013. These projects restored around 275 hectares of laurel forest, which is roughly 680 acres, while later projects continued the restoration in the protected area.This work restored around 1,000 acres of core laurel forest over approximately two decades, with more than 500,000 native trees planted. Specifically, the European Commissionâs LIFE program notes a broader project footprint of roughly 450 hectares (about 1,112 acres) actively managed. This restored core area ultimately acted as an ecological engine, improving environmental quality across the wider region.In 2010, the IUCN moved the species from Critically Endangered to Endangered when a comprehensive, modernised census estimated the population at 1,000 birds, and then to Vulnerable in 2016. These changes indicate that the Azores bullfinch had successfully moved away from its steep downward trajectory and achieved population stabilisation.By 2023, data published by the European Commission reported that the population had grown to around 1,300 individuals. Benefiting from the core restoration work, these birds successfully expanded out into nearly 5,000 acres of suitable regional habitat now available within the wider protected zone. articles.body:
Some offers on this page are from advertisers who pay us, which may affect which products we write about, but not our recommendations. See our Advertiser Disclosure .

Deposit account rates are on the decline — but the good news is you can lock in a competitive return on a certificate of deposit (CD) today and preserve your earning power. In fact, the best CDs still pay rates of 4% or higher. Read on for a snapshot of CD rates today and where to find the best offers.

CDs today typically offer rates significantly higher than traditional savings accounts. Currently, the best short-term CDs (six to 12 months) generally offer rates around 4% APY.

Today, the highest CD rate is 4.30% APY. Synchrony Bank offers this rate on its 16-month CD, and Marcus by Goldman Sachs offers it on its 18-month CD.

The following is a look at some of the best CD rates available today, Tuesday, August 25, 2026 , from our verified partners.

The 2000s were marked by the dot-com bubble and later, the global financial crisis of 2008. Though the early 2000s saw relatively higher CD rates, they began to fall as the economy slowed and the Federal Reserve cut its target rate to stimulate growth. By 2009, in the aftermath of the financial crisis, the average one-year CD paid around 1% APY, with five-year CDs at less than 2% APY.

The trend of falling CD rates continued into the 2010s, especially after the Great Recession of 2007-2009. The Fed's policies to stimulate the economy (in particular, its decision to keep its benchmark interest rate near zero) led banks to offer very low rates on CDs. By 2013, average rates on 6-month CDs fell to about 0.1% APY, while 5-year CDs returned an average of 0.8% APY.

However, things changed between 2015 and 2018, when the Fed started gradually increasing rates again. At this point, there was a slight improvement in CD rates as the economy expanded, marking the end of nearly a decade of ultra-low rates. However, the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in early 2020 led to emergency rate cuts by the Fed, causing CD rates to fall to new record lows.

The situation reversed following the pandemic as inflation began to spiral out of control. This prompted the Fed to hike rates 11 times between March 2022 and July 2023. In turn, this led to higher rates on loans and higher APYs on savings products, including CDs.

Fast forward to September 2024 — the Fed finally decided to start cutting the federal funds rate after it determined that inflation was essentially under control. The Fed cut rates three times in 2025, and we saw CD rates steadily come down from their peak. Even with the Fed leaving interest rates unchanged so far in 2026, CD rates remain high by historical standards.

Take a look at how CD rates have changed since 2009:

Traditionally, longer-term CDs have offered higher interest rates compared to shorter-term CDs. This is because locking in money for a longer period typically carries more risk (namely, missing out on higher rates in the future), which banks compensate for with higher rates.

However, this pattern doesn't necessarily hold today; the highest average CD rate is for a 12-month term. This indicates a flattening or inversion of the yield curve, which can happen in uncertain economic times or when investors expect future interest rates to decline.

When opening a CD , choosing one with a high APY is just one piece of the puzzle. There are other factors that can impact whether a particular CD is best for your needs and your overall return. Consider the following when choosing a CD:

Your goals: Decide how long you're willing to lock away your funds. CDs come with fixed terms, and withdrawing your money before the term ends can result in penalties. Common terms range from a few months up to several years. The right term for you depends on when you anticipate needing access to your money.

Type of financial institution: Rates can vary significantly among financial institutions. Don't just check with your current bank; research CD rates from online banks, local banks, and credit unions. Online banks , in particular, often offer higher interest rates than traditional brick-and-mortar banks because they have lower overhead costs. However, make sure any online bank you consider is FDIC-insured (or NCUA-insured for credit unions).

Account terms: Beyond the interest rate, understand the terms of the CD, including the maturity date and withdrawal penalties . Also, check if there's a minimum deposit requirement, and if so, that it fits your budget.

Inflation: While CDs can offer safe, fixed returns, they might not always keep pace with inflation, especially for longer terms. Consider this when deciding on the term and amount to invest.

articles.title: Rajnath approves transfer of tech of DRDO missile systems to domestic industry to reduce import dependence
articles.summary: News News: NEW DELHI: In a big development to empower Indian private players with new missile technologies to achieve govtâs vision of self-reliance in defence p.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: In a big development to empower Indian private players with new missile technologies to achieve govtâs vision of self-reliance in defence production, defence minister Rajnath Singh has âapproved the transfer of DRDO-developed technologies of all conventional missile systems to the domestic industry for production within the countryâ.Conventional missiles are non-strategic, non-nuclear guided weapon systems designed and developed by DRDO for tactical and traditional battlefield operations. The initiative aims to enhance operational capability, reduce import dependence and increase domestic value addition, while supporting the growth of Indiaâs defence manufacturing sector, a defence ministry statement said on Tuesday.âThough DRDO has already tied up with several defence PSUs and private companies like L&T, Tata Advanced Systems, Bharat Forge and Adani Defence in some missile and defence system programmes, the govt is taking this big step to increase the number of production partners to ensure its supply chain for missiles and their systems are not crippled during the time of conflict in future,â a source in the defence ministry told TOI.DRDO has developed a wide array of conventional (non-strategic) missile systems spanning air defence, strike and anti-armour roles. âThe missiles that are set to become part of technology transfer include surface-to-air missile Akash (can intercept fighter jets, cruise missiles, and drones), Nag (all-weather, fire-and-forget, anti-tank guided missile), Very Short Range Air Defence System (VSHORDS counters low-altitude aerial threats at short ranges); Astra (beyond-visual-range air-to-air missile), Rudram (anti-radiation missile series designed for suppression of enemy air defences) Pralay (short-range, surface-to-surface quasi-ballistic missile) and man-portable ATGM,â the source said.The transfer of technology marks an important milestone in promoting greater participation of the domestic industries in the defence ecosystem by enabling them to undertake indigenous production, as per applicable qualifications, certifications and regulatory requirements, the ministry said.The move has come in the wake of DRDO recently inviting domestic private companies to be âpartner in the development and production of missile and bomb weapon system projects of missiles and strategic systems clusterâ.The objective of the missile tech transfer move is to enhance domestic manufacturing capabilities, strengthen defence industrial base and create opportunities for the participation of Indian MSMEs and other technology partners in the supply chain, it said.The provision will enable successful transition of missile system development to industrial production, reflecting the continued efforts of DRDO to leverage the capabilities of the Indian industry for the development and manufacture of advanced defence systems, the ministry said.

articles.title: In 1993, Minnesota turned 5,000 acres of abandoned iron mines and 15 flooded pits up to 525 feet deep into Cuyuna Country; today the former mining landscape has 50+ miles of bike trails and 25 miles of shoreline
articles.summary: US News: Thirty-three years after local authorities took control of thousands of acres of damaged land, a former mining centre in central Minnesota has complet.
articles.body: Thirty-three years after local authorities took control of thousands of acres of damaged land, a former mining centre in central Minnesota has completed one of the Midwestâs most striking ecological transformations. The Minnesota Department of Natural Resources (MN DNR) established the Cuyuna Country State Recreation Area in 1993, taking over 5,000 acres of abandoned iron mines and 15 flooded open pits. According to state records published in Minnesota Conservation Volunteer magazine, the former industrial site is now a major recreation area with more than 50 miles of singletrack mountain bike trails and 25 miles of natural, undeveloped shoreline.From mining site to recovering landscapeFrom 1900 to the early 1980s, the Cuyuna Iron Range was a major industrial mining area. When mining stopped, companies left behind huge open pits, piles of red earth and old, damaged infrastructure. The unfenced land was also exposed to erosion and safety problems. Over the years, groundwater and rainwater slowly filled the deep mine pits. Fifteen of them became deep, clear lakes, some reaching depths of up to 525 feet. Portsmouth Mine Pit Lake, within the recreation area, became the deepest body of water within Minnesotaâs borders. In 1993, state lawmakers and conservation groups formally created the Cuyuna Country State Recreation Area. The aim was to protect the land from commercial development and housing while restoring the landscape and protecting water quality. The Minnesota DNR developed a long-term plan to allow forests and other vegetation to recover while also opening the area to the public.Turning old mine land into a cycling centreThe transformation into a major cycling destination began after local residents saw the potential in the unusual landscape. According to the Cuyuna Lakes Mountain Bike Crew, the International Mountain Bicycling Association (IMBA) later recognised the area as an official Ride Center. The trail system was designed around the hills and steep changes in elevation created by the old mining waste piles. The area now has several types of trails. More than 50 miles of singletrack mountain bike trails run across the red earth, with routes for beginners as well as experienced riders and downhill cyclists. The recreation area also has 7.5 miles of adaptive trails with wider routes for handcycles and adaptive mountain bikes. The 8-mile paved Cuyuna Lakes State Trail connects communities including Crosby, Ironton and Riverton. During winter, cyclists can use about 40 miles of groomed snow trails for fat biking. The Minnesota DNR says the paved state trail passes through the recreation area and gives visitors access to viewpoints overlooking the flooded mine pits.Community efforts help revive former mining townsRestoring the land also helped bring new life to nearby communities. Historical records from the Parks & Trails Council of Minnesota show that non-profit groups began buying land near the Croft Mine site as early as 1989 to create buffer areas and trailheads. In 1998, local residents created a regional leadership task force to improve public access and connect separate mining areas. A local coalition, including community leaders such as John Schaubach, Bill Bedard and former US Congressman James Oberstar, helped secure land easements and state funding for the growing trail system. "With purpose-built trails for beginners, intermediates and experts, riders from across the region are making the pilgrimage to a new Midwest Mecca," the International Mountain Bicycling Association said during its evaluation of the site. The growth of outdoor tourism has also helped Crosby and Ironton. Former mining supply areas have gradually become centres for bike shops, small hotels, cafes and other businesses serving visitors.Clear lakes offer more than cyclingCycling is not the only attraction. The great depth of the former mine pits and the lack of fine sediment have created unusually clear lakes. Water visibility can often reach more than 30 feet, making the area popular with scuba divers from across the Midwest. The Minnesota DNR manages 25 miles of shoreline around the six natural lakes and 15 mine pit lakes within the recreation area. Anglers can fish for rainbow trout, northern pike, smallmouth bass and walleye. Visitors can also use public boat launches and kayak access points. The 25-site Portsmouth Campground provides another way to stay close to the lakes without large commercial developments along the shoreline. Under the Minnesota DNRâs management plan, the area is meant to remain largely non-commercial. Private housing and intensive timber harvesting along the waterâs edge are not allowed. Today, the Cuyuna Range is a strong example of how damaged industrial land can be reclaimed. What was once a major iron-mining landscape has become a public recreation and ecological asset, with its old pits, red earth and abandoned mining terrain now supporting forests, clear lakes, wildlife and outdoor tourism.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1932, an Ohio foundry worker lost his job and began building a rock garden; he spent 12 years creating hundreds of structures, and his wife preserved it for another 53 years
articles.summary: US News: When Harry George \"Ben\" Hartman lost his job as an iron moulder at the Springfield Machine Tool Company during the Great Depression, he picked up a tr.
articles.body: When Harry George "Ben" Hartman lost his job as an iron moulder at the Springfield Machine Tool Company during the Great Depression, he picked up a trowel and began digging a small concrete fishing pond in his backyard. That simple project soon grew across his entire residential lot. Over 12 years, Hartman built a huge folk art environment using more than 250,000 stones, concrete, metal scraps, wood and recycled glass. After his death in 1944, his wife Mary cared for the entire complex on her own for 53 years, protecting what became one of the leading folk art environments in the United States. According to documentation from the Friends of the Hartman Rock Garden and the Kohler Foundation, the property at 1905 Russell Avenue contains dozens of detailed stone structures, miniature landmarks and hundreds of hand-painted figures representing American history, religion, patriotism and popular culture.From factory job to backyard creationBorn in Edenville, Pennsylvania, in 1882, Hartman moved to Springfield, Ohio, in 1912 to work in the city's heavy machinery foundries. The economic collapse of 1932 ended his industrial career. Suddenly unemployed, Hartman turned his energy towards physical work and began transforming his suburban backyard into a massive construction project. Educational materials prepared for tours of the site say Hartman collected materials from nearby creek beds, rubbish dumps and gravel roads. He often asked his children to collect unusual stones, while friends and local visitors brought discarded glass bottles and pieces of ceramics that he used in the structures. Hartman spent long hours building the garden even after developing severe silicosis, a lung disease caused by years of exposure to dust in foundries. When he died from the illness in 1944 at the age of 61, the garden had spread across the entire residential yard.Architecture, patriotism and personal expressionThe centrepiece of the garden is the Tree of Life, a seven-foot concrete structure covered with river gravel and polished stones. Its branches hold miniature versions of a schoolhouse and church, while two doves of peace sit on either side and a carved American eagle stands at the top. Historical archives maintained by SPACES (Saving and Preserving Arts and Cultural Environments) show that Hartman also built several large architectural replicas directly on the lawn. One of the largest is The Cathedral, a 14-foot-high medieval-style stone building with detailed arches, niches and handmade figures of Jesus, Mary and several saints. The garden also contains scale models of Mount Vernon and the White House, as well as a replica of the Independence Hall clock tower. Hartman created other structures honouring figures including Abraham Lincoln, George Washington and Charles Lindbergh. The garden also includes stone versions of Noah's Ark and covered wagons representing the Oregon Trail. Other parts of the garden show everyday American life, with miniature stone houses, bridges and working water wheels. "This is where it all began, this is the Hobby gone wild," folk art collector Mark Chepp said during a historical tour recorded by public radio station WYSO. "Ben was a pacifist, and as you go through the garden and get involved and start looking at it, you see social commentary that comes through in a number of the objects."53 years of careAfter Hartman's death in 1944, his wife Mary took responsibility for the garden. articles.title: EasyJet holiday: Dozens stranded in Tunisia after Belfast flight cancelled
articles.summary: One man says he has spent more than £4,000 to get his family of five home after being told they may have to wait 10 days for another flight.
articles.body:
Dozens of people from Northern Ireland have been left stranded in Tunisia after their EasyJet flight home was cancelled, with the airline telling them it had no other flights available for another 10 days.

One man told BBC News NI he has spent £4,000 on travel home for his family-of-five, while another woman, Georgina Doherty, said she and her six children were trying to get home after the death of her mother-in-law.

Others described running out of medication for health issues, while EasyJet were also criticised over a lack of support and communication.

EasyJet has said it is operating an additional direct flight to Belfast on Tuesday night, and that it was "very sorry" for the inconvenience.

BBC News NI understands more than 100 people were booked onto the cancelled flight that was due to leave Enfidha-Hamamet Airport for Belfast International three days ago.

Stuart McCartney, from Dromore, County Down, said he had spent thousands on accommodation and flights to get his family home via a flight to Brussels.

"I'm willing to pay £4,000 to get us home, if needs be, and then battle for reimbursement if I have to after that," he said.

"But we shouldn't have to pay. My holiday was a fraction of what I'm paying to get home right now."

McCartney said EasyJet provided two nights of accommodation but then told the family to find alternative accommodation for the rest of the delay.

He said his mother Katherine, who accompanied his wife and children on the trip, relies on heart medication and they have had to keep a close eye on her remaining supply as the delay continued.

An EasyJet spokesperson said that the company "have been doing everything we can to support Mr McCartney, providing hotel accommodation and meals and we will be reimbursing expenses that may have been incurred".

Georgina Doherty, who is originally from Londonderry but now lives in County Donegal, told BBC News NI the last few days have been an "absolute nightmare" for her family.

Her husband returned home a day before they were due to fly back due to his mother taking ill. She has since died, with Doherty and her six children stranded in Tunisia.

What happened to the EasyJet flight from Tunisia to Belfast?

McCartney said passengers had completed the normal departure process on Saturday night, collecting their boarding passes and gathering at the gate before the flight was called off after more than two hours of delays.

He said the pilot told passengers the aircraft had a number of technical problems, including an issue affecting its steering.

He said "tired and anxious" passengers were eventually taken through the airport in the early hours of Sunday morning and transported by bus to separate hotels.

When he returned to the airport on Sunday, McCartney said an EasyJet agent was only able to look at the airline's own options and could not find a route that would get his family home sooner.

With his children due to return to school and the adults expected back at work, he looked for an alternative. The family are now booked on flights from Tunisia to Brussels, followed by a seven-hour layover before travelling on to Dublin on Wednesday.

He said the uncertainty had taken an emotional toll on his family, particularly his children - he said his son, who is due to return to school and rugby training school, "broke down badly" when he learned of the delay.

Meanwhile, passengers have been supporting each other, he added, helping with transport, translation and finding alternative routes home.

"The camaraderie with people is unbelievable," he added.

"We all are trying so hard for each other."

Like Stuart McCartney, Georgina Doherty and her six children, aged from four to 16, were given two nights accommodation.

On the third day, she said they were told they would have to check out or pay up front for the remainder of our stay.

That would have cost upwards of €3,700 (£3,170), she said.

Doherty said all this was happening as she was trying to tell her children that their "granny had died".

"You couldn't actually have time to process it because we were so stressed out trying to secure the accommodation for the seven of us.

"You couldn't script it, what has happened," she said.

Like many of the passengers, she said, her family has felt abandoned by the airline.

"There has been a complete blackout of communication."

Martine Murray from Belfast, said she is desperate to return home because her mother is seriously ill.

She said she has had to borrow money from friends and family to pay for alternative accommodation after leaving a hotel arranged by EasyJet, which she described as dirty.

"I don't have that money, but I'll have to pay it back," she said.

Murray also has COPD and has run out of her inhaler.

She said she had received an email informing her that her flight had been cancelled, but had been unable to get further information from the airline despite trying to contact it.

"Get us home, we need to get home now," she said.

"I would never travel with them (EasyJet) again."

Natasha Dovbijenko, who is travelling with her husband and child, said the hotel provided by EasyJet was very dirty, with bathrooms that did not work.

Dovbijenko added there was then "a lot of back and forth" over their travel arrangements, including an attempt to separate her from her husband, before they eventually secured a flight to Liverpool.

From there, they had to arrange their own travel back to Ireland.

"There's been no contact from EasyJet, just a message that night saying sorry to hear your flight was cancelled," she said.

"They've treated us very bad. No contact. EasyJet have basically just left us."

EasyJet said the flight to Belfast on 23 August "experienced a technical issue and was unable to operate".

A spokesperson added: "We have been doing everything we can to support our customers, providing hotel accommodation and meals and we will be reimbursing expenses that may have been incurred.

"As alternative flight options including with other carriers are very limited at this busy time of year, we will be operating an additional direct flight from Enfidha to Belfast this evening and providing onward transfers home where needed," the spokeperson said.

The airline said it would be contacting customers directly with the information on the flight.

"A dedicated number - 03305515147 - is also available for customers in Enfidha who require assistance. easyJet holidays customers are also being contacted directly," the spokeperson said.

"The welfare of our customers is our highest priority and we are very sorry for the inconvenience caused."

articles.title: Nigeria kidnappings: President Bola Tinubu orders manhunt after victim video uploaded
articles.summary: The footage shows dozens of men, women and children sitting in a forest.
articles.body:
Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu has ordered a manhunt for armed kidnappers who launched deadly attacks on four villages in a remote part of Niger state last Friday.

Local residents told the BBC several mosques were simultaneously targeted during prayers. A local youth leader says as many as 500 people may have been abducted, though this has not been verified.

The president's orders came after the kidnappers posted a video on social media of what they said were those abducted last week sitting in a forest.

The authorities had previously suspected the attackers were bandits - criminal gangs involved in kidnapping and looting for ransom across parts of Nigeria.

The kidnap gangs, jihadists and separatists wreaking havoc in Nigeria

The gunmen, reportedly dressed in military-style clothing, attacked the villages of Dekara, Gidan Zana, Sabon Gida and Masaka.

Police spokesman Wasiu Abiodun told the BBC that more than 40 people were killed, but the exact number of deaths had not been confirmed.

Looking at the footage released on social media, the local youth leader, who asked not to be named, said he recognised several individuals from his community.

"I was able to identify many people. There is an elderly man in the video who is like a grandfather to us," he said. "He lives in Gidan Zana village."

He said families who had spotted relatives in the video were relieved to know they were still alive.

"At least they know where their loved ones are and hope they may be rescued, unlike those who still have no information about missing relatives," he added.

A local blogger familiar with the area told the BBC that many residents had fled their homes, seeking refuge in neighbouring states or across the border in Benin.

Some survivors are receiving hospital treatment, including people with serious injuries.

A local official also told the BBC that the attackers planted improvised explosive devices in parts of the affected communities as they led abductees into the forest. He said a teenage boy was killed when an explosive detonated as he tried to escape.

In a statement issued by presidential spokesman Bayo Onanuga, Tinubu condemned the killings and abductions and vowed that those responsible would be brought to justice.

"Those who carried out this cowardly attack on defenceless Nigerians are enemies of peace and enemies of humanity, who will not go scot-free," the statement said.

The president also expressed his condolences to the families of those killed.

The attack is the latest sign of worsening insecurity in the Borgu area, which borders Kebbi and Kwara states as well as neighbouring Benin.

Earlier this month, police said 145 people had been rescued after being abducted from four other villages in the area.

Local officials have also raised concerns about the growing presence of jihadist groups operating in parts of north-western Nigeria and along the border region, saying some fighters have recently entered communities and imposed religious restrictions on residents.

articles.title: West Bank settlers attack AFP journalists
articles.summary: Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank on Tuesday attacked AFP journalists reporting on tension with Palestinians, in violence that left at least five pe...
articles.body:
Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank on Tuesday attacked AFP journalists reporting on tension with Palestinians, in violence that left at least five people injured, the reporters and medics said.

A three-person team from the international news agency had travelled to the village of Jannatah near Bethlehem to report on Israeli activists who conduct solidarity visits to support Palestinians facing harassment by Israeli settlers, who recently blocked a road in the area.

After an altercation broke out between the settlers and activists, the Israeli military ordered journalists to leave what it called a "closed military zone", at which point two additional cars full of settlers swooped in.

The settlers, many of them children, threw stones towards the journalists and activists. One AFP journalist ducked a stone but then a child settler struck him in the chin with a stick, causing minor bleeding, he said.

The AFP journalists returned to see their two parked cars both damaged, with back windshields smashed in and tyres punctured. Activists' cars suffered similar damage.

Five people were treated for injuries, the Palestine Red Crescent Society said, with AFP journalists reporting seeing at least one Israeli activist taken in a Palestinian ambulance.

During the clash an Israeli soldier temporarily seized the camera of a video journalist but handed it back afterward, the AFP journalists said.

An Israeli military spokesperson said that the temporary confiscation of the camera "is currently being reviewed".

Israeli police joined the military to collect evidence on the damage to cars and "a police investigation has been opened into the incident", the military spokesperson said.

More than 500,000 Israelis live in the West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967, home to around three million Palestinians, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing government advancing more construction ahead of October 27 elections.

Violence against Palestinians by Israeli settlers has increased dramatically since the October 7, 2023 attack on Israel by Hamas from the Gaza Strip.

articles.title: What's the $1,000 savings challenge, and how does it work?
articles.summary: The $1,000 savings challenge helps you prioritize saving money and reach your first big milestone. Here's how the $1,000 savings challenge works and tips for...
articles.body:
Some offers on this page are from advertisers who pay us, which may affect which products we write about, but not our recommendations. See our Advertiser Disclosure .

Saving can be tough, but focusing on a specific goal can help.

The $1,000 savings challenge is a self-directed strategy to focus your efforts. It gives you a reasonable target to boost your savings, regardless of what you're saving for.

There's no one right way to complete the $1,000 savings challenge, so you're free to make it your own. Continue reading for tips on how to structure the challenge and what to do with your savings after reaching your goal.

What's the $1,000 savings challenge, and how does it work?

The $1,000 savings challenge is precisely what it sounds like — a way to challenge yourself to save $1,000 within a set time frame. Saving $1,000 can help you reach a range of financial goals, or it can be a way to jumpstart your savings journey.

There's no single right way to structure the $1,000 savings challenge — whether you aim to save $1,000 in one month or one year, the point is the same: To prioritize saving money consistently over time. Here are a few steps to get you started:

Set a deadline. A deadline can provide some healthy urgency to reach your goal. Choose a deadline that feels challenging yet reasonable. Depending on your income and budget, that could be a month, a year, or somewhere in between.

Designate a place for your savings. Pick a place for your savings so you can track progress toward your goal. Some people prefer seeing physical cash add up in an envelope or a jar. That said, a savings account is more secure and convenient. Plus, it'll earn interest that helps your balance grow even faster.

Break down your goal by week or month. Breaking down your goal into bite-sized pieces can make it feel more doable. Using your deadline, figure out how much you need to save each week or month to reach your $1,000 goal. For example, if you want to save $1,000 in six months, you'll need to save about $167 per month.

Tips for completing the $1,000 savings challenge

Completing the $1,000 savings challenge may not be easy, but staying focused on your goal can help. Use the following tips to keep your goal in sight, track your progress, and stay motivated along the way.

Saving money is an important habit — but where you put those savings also matters. Letting your savings sit in the bank without working for you leaves money on the table.

A high-yield savings account (HYSA) is a type of account that pays a higher interest rate than a traditional savings account, allowing your earnings to compound at a faster rate. In fact, the best high-yield savings accounts earn as much as 4% APY today. Plus, your money remains secure and relatively easy to access.

So, as you work on completing your goal of saving $1,000, deposit your money into an HYSA where it can gain interest and grow even faster.

Cutting down some of your monthly expenses can help speed up your savings progress. But if you don't have a budget in place, you might not know where you're overspending.

Creating a budget can make the $1,000 savings challenge more manageable because it shows you exactly how much money you have available to save and where you might be able to free up additional cash.

You can only cut so much from your spending, but you can always earn more. Negotiate a raise, sell used clothes, have a garage sale, or launch a side hustle to give your savings a boost.

Automating your savings contributions can essentially guarantee your success. Set up recurring transfers from your checking account into your savings account to put progress on autopilot. Just make sure you have the funds to do so to avoid overdrawing your account.

There are countless money-saving apps on the market. For example, some include a feature that allows you to round up transactions to the nearest dollar and stash the extra change in your savings account. Others may offer rewards on eligible purchases that you can put toward your savings goal.

Just pay attention to subscription fees and other costs. An app should help you save more than it costs you to use.

articles.title: Hydel project shutdown triggers power crisis in J&K
articles.summary: India News: SRINAGAR: Jammu & Kashmir is grappling with power shortages and unscheduled outages after key hydroelectric projects, including the 450MW Baglihar.
articles.body: SRINAGAR: Jammu & Kashmir is grappling with power shortages and unscheduled outages after key hydroelectric projects, including the 450MW Baglihar stage I and the Salal project, were shut for silt-flushing operations. Baglihar stage-I in Ramban district has remained non-operational for a week, with accumulated silt at its gates delaying restoration work.Officials said desilting work at Baglihar stages I and II and the Salal project began on Aug 18. While Baglihar stage II resumed generation on Aug 22, stage I is yet to restart. Salal is expected to resume operations on Tuesday.The prolonged shutdown has widened the regionâs power deficit. Jammu & Kashmirâs peak electricity demand stands at about 2,500MW in summer and 3,000MW in winter. With both Baglihar units largely unavailable for most of the past week, Jammu & Kashmir faced a shortfall of nearly 900MW.Built on the Chenab river, Baglihar stages I and II are among Jammu & Kashmirâs key power sources. Following the disruption, the power department is exploring alternative arrangements to bridge the supply gap.The crisis comes amid criticism of the Omar Abdullah-led govt over rising electricity tariffs. From Sept 1, power consumers in Jammu & Kashmir will face a 6.83% tariff hike.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Liberia's ex-vice president will await trial on drug trafficking and other charges in prison
articles.summary: Liberia's former vice president was sent to prison on Tuesday to await trial on drug trafficking and other charges, after a court in the West African country...
articles.body:
MONROVIA, Liberia (AP) — Liberia's former vice president was sent to prison on Tuesday to await trial on drug trafficking and other charges, after a court in the West African country denied her request to be released on humanitarian grounds for medical treatment.

Jewel Howard-Taylor's lawyers asked the court for her to remain at a local hospital in Monrovia to receive treatment for a health emergency. She suffered an asthma attack and her blood pressure was high while in police custody after her arrest, according to local media reports.

Alongside three other foreign nationals charged in absentia, the former vice president and wife of former president, Charles Taylor, is facing multiple charges for drug trafficking, money laundering and other offenses as part of an investigation into an alleged transnational narcotics network. Howard-Taylor was vice president from 2018 to 2024.

She was arrested on Aug. 19 at Roberts International Airport while she was attempting to leave Liberia.

Her lawyers have rejected the allegations, saying they are politically motivated, but investigators say the case is supported by travel records, audio recordings, witness testimonies and evidence of her alleged association with members of the transnational cocaine trafficking network.

Last month, Liberian authorities seized and burned around 4.2 metric tons of cocaine with a street value estimated to be about $317 million, also implicating some senior police officials in the trafficking operation, which has been linked to her.

In recent years, West Africa has emerged as a key transit route for cocaine trafficked from South America to Europe, with smugglers taking advantage of porous borders and weak enforcement in parts of the region.

articles.title: Revised bullet train cost Rs 2 lakh crore, 2x of original estimate
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The cost of the Ahmedabad-Mumbai bullet train has been revised to around Rs 2.1 lakh crore, nearly double the original cost of approximatel.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The cost of the Ahmedabad-Mumbai bullet train has been revised to around Rs 2.1 lakh crore, nearly double the original cost of approximately Rs 1.1 lakh crore. The proposal to seek approval for the revised cost of the 508-km high-speed rail line was placed before the Cabinet Tuesday, TOI has learnt.Sources said the railway ministry has cited the time taken in land acquisition in Maharashtra and delay in getting the train sets from Japan as among the main reasons for the cost escalation. They added the project is likely to be completed in 2030 and the first leg of the corridor is scheduled to be operational in Aug 2027.Sources said most of the additional funding would come from budgetary support. So far, the funding of Rs 1.1 lakh crore has been from Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) and budgetary allocation. They added that Railways has said high-speed trains will be manufactured in India and each of these would cost around Rs 390 crore to Rs 400 crore. There was no official briefing on the decisions of the Cabinet meeting chaired by PM Narendra Modi.In Jan, railway board chairperson Satish Kumar had said the project cost had increased by around 83% to Rs 1.98 lakh crore. The project has faced time and cost overruns due to many reasons, including delay in land acquisition, statutory clearances and finalisation of the trains.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Tuesday sought the Union govtâs response to US-based octogenarian â Khalid Jahangir Qazi â an OCI card holder accused .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Tuesday sought the Union govtâs response to US-based octogenarian â Khalid Jahangir Qazi â an OCI card holder accused by India of peddling pro-Pakistan propaganda and being sympathetic to Kashmiri separatists, who is seeking permission to visit Kashmir to attend wedding functions in his sisterâs family.Appearing for Qazi, whose OCI card cancellation was annulled by a single judge bench of Delhi high court and appeals against which is pending before a division bench, senior advocate Parag Tripathi told a bench led by CJI Surya Kant that the 82-year-old medical practitioner had visited India in the past and given his age and that of his relatives, this may be the last time he would be able to visit Kashmir and be with family members.âHe is ready to give an undertaking that during his visit, he would not indulge in any political activity,â Tripathi said. This persuaded the bench to issue notice to the Centre and sought its response by Sep 7, the next date of hearing. The Delhi high court had earlier rejected his plea to visit India.Qazi stands accused of âpro-Pakistan propagandaâ by the Indian Consulate in New York. Indian govt had cancelled his OCI card in May 2023 because of activities which are âinimical to sovereignty and security of Indiaâ, and blacklisted him under the Foreigners Act. In Nov 2024, a single judge bench of the Delhi HC had quashed the cancellation of his OCI card saying that Qazi was not given a fair hearing prior to the cancellation.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A couple built a four-bedroom home in Wiltshire for their disabled daughter in 2022, now face council demolition order after planning row over basement and Green Belt rules
articles.summary: UK News: A Wiltshire couple have been ordered to demolish the four-bedroom home they have lived in with their disabled daughter for more than four years after .
articles.body: A Wiltshire couple have been ordered to demolish the four-bedroom home they have lived in with their disabled daughter for more than four years after a planning dispute over the property's basement and decking.According to a report published by The Wiltshire Gazette and Herald, Pim and Sheree de Witte built the hillside property at Little Orchard in Kingdown, between Corsham and Bath. The house, which replaced an earlier dwelling on the site, was completed and occupied in 2022.The couple are now appealing to the Planning Inspectorate after Wiltshire Council refused retrospective planning permission for the house as built. The appeal has put the enforcement notice requiring demolition on hold.Couple say basement was needed for disabled daughterThe de Wittes were originally granted planning permission in 2019 for a replacement dwelling with ground and first-floor levels. However, the completed property included an additional basement level and a decking area.The couple say the basement was constructed as part of the foundations for engineering reasons and was not an arbitrary addition. They subsequently converted the space into residential accommodation for their disabled daughter.They argue that the property remains a replacement dwelling rather than a new-build home and maintain that the original planning permission was lawfully implemented.The couple have also argued that the need to provide suitable accommodation for their disabled daughter should be considered a "material consideration" in the planning decision.Council says house breaches Green Belt policyThe property is located within the Green Belt, and Wiltshire Council has argued that the house as built is materially larger than the dwelling it replaced.A planning application submitted in 2024 seeking to regularise the changes was refused.The couple returned to the council in 2025 with another proposal. Under the revised plans, part of the basement floor area would have been sealed off and concealed by depositing soil around it. The size of the decking would also have been reduced.However, the council rejected the proposal, saying the dwelling remained materially larger than the one it replaced and conflicted with Green Belt policy.The council also said the application failed to demonstrate material considerations or special circumstances that could outweigh the harm identified.Couple call council's approach "harsh and punitive"The de Wittes have criticised the council's decision, describing its response as "unnecessarily harsh and punitive given the individual circumstances and merits of this case."They have now taken their case to the Planning Inspectorate, which will consider whether the property can remain.The couple have also proposed alternative solutions if their appeal is dismissed, including reinstating the house to its previously approved form.Demolition order put on holdIn February this year, the couple were ordered to demolish the property by the end of August. Their appeal has since put that enforcement action on hold while the planning inspector considers the case.The dispute centres on whether the additional basement and decking amount to a breach of the planning permission and whether the circumstances of the family, particularly the accommodation needs of their disabled daughter, provide sufficient grounds for the changes to be retained.A decision from the Planning Inspectorate is expected in the autumn.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
