articles.title: UK weather: Met Office warnings in force amid thunderstorm and flood risk
articles.summary: Torrential downpours will affect parts of England and Wales, delivering some of the wettest weather in several weeks
articles.body:
Downpours and thunderstorms will continue to bring the risk of flooding to parts of the UK on Wednesday.

A Met Office yellow warning for thunderstorms is valid from 03:00 until 22:00 BST, covering much of the Midlands, parts of northern, eastern and southern England, as well as the far east of Wales.

The rain could be heavy enough to bring flash flooding and travel disruption, with lightning and large hail posing additional hazards.

A further Met Office yellow warning has been issued for Thursday with more thunderstorms expected.

For some areas that have seen barely any rain so far this August, the next few days could bring the wettest weather in many weeks.

The Met Office yellow thunderstorm warning covers a large swathe of England and Wales.

A band of showers and thunderstorms will push northwards during Wednesday morning with sunny spells following from the south.

However, further scattered downpours and storms will spring up during the afternoon.

As many as 20-30mm (0.8-1.2in) of rain could fall in some locations within just an hour, and it is even possible that 40-50mm (1.6-2in) could accumulate over a few hours.

However, due to the hit-and-miss nature of showers, some places will miss the rain and weather apps may struggle to get the detail of the forecast correct.

Where the rain does fall, flash flooding is a real concern. This will be especially problematic where the ground is hard after the prolonged dry spell, making it difficult for the water to soak in.

Difficult driving conditions are expected with the chance that some roads could be closed.

Large hail and frequent lightning are also possible.

Northern Ireland will also see some showers but these are likely to be less intense with less thunder.

Many parts of Scotland will remain dry with sunny spells, although some showers are likely in the south-west later.

Thursday will bring another zone of thunderstorms, again affecting mostly England and Wales.

The Met Office has issued a further yellow weather warning, valid from 06:00 until 22:00 BST.

Widespread rainfall totals of 20-30mm (0.8-1.2in) are expected in the warning area within three hours, while some areas could see 50mm (2in) within the same timeframe.

There is a small chance that eastern-facing hills - exposed to easterly winds - could record 75mm (3in) during 12 hours, which would bring a significant flood risk.

The showers may eventually reach southern Scotland and Northern Ireland but are likely to weaken and become less intense as they drift northwards.

Wettest weather in weeks for parts of southern UK

Despite a period of unsettled weather last week, some southern parts of the UK have still seen barely any rain recently.

Brize Norton in Oxfordshire has recorded just 0.4mm of rain so far this August, less than 1% of what it would normally expect during the month as a whole.

Kew Gardens recorded no rain at all in July, and only 1.8mm so far this month.

It means the rain we are expecting this week is likely to far outstrip what has fallen recently in some areas.

What does 80 per cent chance of rain mean?

Why you may not see showers and thunderstorms on your weather app

Thunderstorms are often very hit-and-miss.

Some places can see flooding downpours while others, perhaps only a few miles away, avoid the heaviest rain and stay essentially dry.

Weather apps - including the BBC Weather app - can struggle in these scenarios.

Forecasters know that the conditions are ripe for storms to form, with warm humid air across the UK interacting with a zone of colder air pushing in from the west, higher in the atmosphere.

This generates low pressure and instability.

However, the computer weather models that drive weather apps will always struggle to pinpoint exactly where and when the biggest storms will spring up.

It is a bit like heating popcorn kernels in a pan.

You cannot know precisely which kernels will pop and in which order, while some kernels may not pop at all.

Some of the storms will also occur at night, which may mean they do not show up in the daily weather icons.

It is worth keeping an eye on the hourly weather symbols, as well as the percentage chances of rain, if you are making outdoor plans.

articles.title: N.J. restaurant writes ‘happy wheelchair birthday’ on disabled customer’s dessert. Here’s what we know.
articles.summary: A birthday celebration ended with an unsettling message.
articles.body:
A birthday dinner at an upscale New Jersey restaurant took an unexpected turn when dessert arrived at the table with an insensitive message.

Antonia Sinibaldi , a Hudson County native who suffered a spinal injury in a car crash when she was 2 years old, spent her 29th birthday at Blu on the Hudson back in June with her friends and family.

When Sinibaldi's dessert arrived at the table, next to a lit candle was a message written in icing: "happy wheelchair birthday!"

"It took me by surprise," Sinibaldi, who has relied on a motorized wheelchair and ventilator for most of her life, told CBS News . "I shouldn't be reminded of something that I already know."

The Weehawken resident told CBS News she asked management for an explanation, but was unsatisfied with their response.

"He offered to send me more drinks, more drinks, more drinks," Sinibaldi told CBS News. "What good will that do?"

Sinibaldi declined comment at time of publishing. Messages left for Blu on the Hudson were not returned.

In a statement given to CBS News, Blu on the Hudson apologized for the incident.

"We at Blu on the Hudson are aware of the recent video circulating on social media, and we are deeply saddened by what occurred. We sincerely apologize to the guest and to everyone who was hurt or offended by this incident which took place on June 20, 2026. Treating every guest with dignity, respect, and care is fundamental to who we are as a company."

The statement went on to provide further context for the incident, noting Blu on the Hudson's staff uses tables and seat numbers to identify where dishes are delivered. "Wheelchair" was used as a reference for where the birthday dessert with a candle was to be delivered, but was not intended to be written on the plate.

"There was absolutely no malicious or disrespectful intent behind the notation," the statement read. "However, we fully understand how seeing that word written on a plate could be deeply hurtful and upsetting."

Blu on the Hudson also said in the statement it has since talked to the staff about the importance of proper ticketing and communication, in hopes of making sure an incident like this doesn't happen again. The restaurant said it also unsuccessfully attempted to reconnect with Sinibaldi to apologize further.

articles.title: Jewish, Muslim, Christian Jerusalem Old City vendors say reduced tourism is harming businesses
articles.summary: Vendors pointed to a shortage of flights, high airfares, and lingering fears abroad about security as the main reasons traffic into Israel has suffered. Shop...
articles.body:
Vendors pointed to a shortage of flights, high airfares, and lingering fears abroad about security as the main reasons traffic into Israel has suffered.

Shopkeepers across the Jewish, Muslim, Christian, and Armenian quarters of Jerusalem's Old City say the weakened state of inbound tourism to Israel over the last three years, since the outbreak of war, has put businesses under prolonged strain.

Speaking this week to The Jerusalem Post , vendors pointed to a shortage of flights, high airfares, and lingering fears abroad over security as chief reasons traffic into Israel has been suffering.

"The day-to-day tourism is horrible," Eitan, the owner of Mira, a family-owned shop in the Jewish Quarter, said. "Not too many people. There's not the traffic that there should be."

The main problem, he said, was that there were a reduced number of flights and that the flights that were operating were too expensive for many people, and people are afraid to come."

"I know a lot of people who cancel their — like, sometimes the airline canceled their trip, sometimes they could not come because of the prices," he said. "Once you have limited seats available, not everybody can come."

Eitan, whose family has lived in the Old City since 1968, operated the business since 1984, and has been through "all the intifadas" and "all the wars," said that a meaningful recovery from the tourism slump will remain out of sight until the situation with the airlines improves.

"As long as the airlines are not coming back to Israel, I don't see any solution," he said.

Similar concerns were voiced elsewhere in the Old City.

Dia, a long-time vendor in Jerusalem's Old City Arab Quarter whose family operates the well-known "Alabama – The Heart of Dixie" shop, said the decline in tourism had left business "very, very slow," with many visitors still hesitant to come because of the war.

"It's very safe, the Old City," he said, but due to the image Israel has had abroad since the war began on October 7, 2023, business remained low.

"Three years now, nobody comes," he said.

Hassan, a souvenir vendor near the Church of the Holy Sepulcher in Jerusalem's Christian Quarter, also painted a negative picture, describing business as "very weak" and saying there were "no tourists now."

He recalled that before the war broke out, there was a period of eight to ten months when business was good, "but now, it's zero."

Hassan continued, saying that in his view, the solution lay in bolstering the number of flights coming into Israel.

In the Armenian Quarter, Garo Sandrouni, who operates a ceramics gallery with his wife, Sonia, said that even since the latest major round of strikes between Israel and Iran concluded earlier this year, he had not seen any improvement in the number of tourists coming through.

He said, though, that with the Jewish New Year coming up next month, vendors expected to see some progress.

"Now, everybody is expecting in September that it (the amount of inbound tourism) will be much more. Let's see. But now, there is not much difference from what it was like three months ago or four months ago."

Like other vendors, Garo pointed to the cost of flights as the primary barrier choking off tourism to the country.

"They're much more expensive than before, and some people are also afraid to come," he said.

Sandrouni added that the fear came from three places.

"People are afraid, first from the war, secondly from flights if they cancel, and thirdly from the expensive tickets," he said.

He recalled clients who became stranded in Israel after foreign carriers canceled service, with some eventually traveling to Jordan to fly home.

Sandrouni added that the hits his business has taken over the last three years have been the worst in his four decades of operations.

"I have been here for like 40, 45 years on this street," he said. "It is the worst thing that we have witnessed. I mean, from the October war until today."

Speaking to the Post in June, tourism expert Dr. Eran Ketter pointed to broad structural problems hampering inbound tourism to Israel.

Looking specifically at the US, historically Israel's largest source market, Ketter pointed to geopolitical instability, the stronger shekel, limited air capacity, and higher travel costs as factors suppressing demand.

Tourism expert: Problems around tourism limit visitors to just the highly committed

"Putting all of this together, we're coming into a situation that only people who really want to travel to Israel, and can afford it, are traveling at the moment," he said.

Ketter said greater political stability would be the "number one enabler," allowing the industry to move from a nearly three-year "survival state" into "growth mode."

Stability, he added, would also encourage airlines to resume service, bringing more competition and potentially cheaper fares.

Tourism Ministry Director-General Michael Izhakov , who spoke to the Post the following month, also identified the lack of flight accessibility as a major bottleneck to inbound tourism.

Tourism ministry director-general: With no flights, there is no tourism

"When there are no flights, there is no tourism," he said, adding that the ministry was speaking with airlines and the Transportation Ministry and expected a rapid recovery once flights returned.

"We are waiting only for the flights," he said. "Once the flights reopen, we will see a very rapid recovery in inbound tourism to Israel."

The ministry has also been trying to stimulate demand through marketing and domestic tourism while preparing additional hotel capacity. Izhakov said the ministry had begun targeting Jewish audiences abroad more directly and had shifted some attention toward Israeli tourists when foreign visitors failed to return.

Earlier this month, Izhakov and tourism industry leaders met US Ambassador Mike Huckabee as part of the Israel Tourism Recovery Forum, where, according to the ministry, they discussed expanding direct US-Israel flights.

During the meeting, Huckabee emphasized his personal commitment to promote trips from the US to Israel.

"I will continue encouraging Americans to visit Israel, experience it firsthand, and discover the reality for themselves," the ministry quoted the ambassador as saying.

For the vendors in the Old City who depend on this traffic, though, the recovery of inbound tourism and the expansion of flights into the country are things they say cannot wait.

Still, despite the economic situation they described, some remained optimistic.

"I'm a positive person," Eitan said. "I believe things will be good again. When, we don't know, but hopefully soon. We are here, and whatever God wants to give us, he gives us."

articles.title: Steve Sarkisian expounds on second scrimmage issues
articles.summary: The Longhorns have areas to improve upon on both sides of the ball.
articles.body:
AUSTIN, Texas — For the second straight scrimmage during preseason camp, the Texas Longhorns defense got the best of the offense at Darrell K Royal-Texas Memorial Stadium in a 120-play game simulation impacted by brutal heat as the temperature on Campbell-Williams Field reached closed to 150 degrees.

During a Monday media availability, Texas head coach Steve Sarkisian expounded on the areas that his team needs to improve upon before the 2:30 p.m. Central kickoff against Texas State on Sept. 5.

"What I was trying to get at Saturday from an offensive perspective, it felt a little, I guess, lethargic is the best word for what we've been in practice, for how good of a week they had, and so we've got to do a better job from an offensive coach's perspective of making sure the mentality is right when we're in those conditions," Sarkisian said.

With a current forecast high of 99 degrees for the opener, the heat will only be slightly less intense, increasing the already high level of scrutiny on the team's depth that the Longhorns will need against the Bobcats to keep players fresh, including for the high-profile tilt against the Buckeyes the following week.

Missed assignments were also an issue for the offense, ranging from improperly alignment to blocking the wrong person to running the wrong route or the right route at the wrong depth.

"Things that we have done well for two and a half weeks time, and all of a sudden we got into that arena and we made some some mistakes that were uncharacteristic to us, so we've got to get to the bottom of that," Sarkisian said.

The MAs weren't the only mental mistakes on Sarkisian's side of the ball, either.

"Too many times — I use the term we played mindless football offensively — we were running plays rather than playing football in a competitive setting, playing the game of football. It's different when you're in practice and it's all scripted, and you run the play, whatever happens, the ball goes to the right hash, and you run the next play," Sarkisian said.

"When you get into a scrimmage, you're trying to make it as game-like as possible — there's consequences for not doing things right. It may be a sack, it may be a false start, it may be a missed block, whatever that looks like. We we can't play mindless football when we get into scrimmage and game settings. We need to apply the game to the play and the play to the game."

The offense also left some plays on the field as the quarterbacks missed opportunities for explosive pass plays.

And even though the defense won the scrimmage, coordinator Will Muschamp's group is still going through some growing pains after losing key communicator Michael Taaffe to the NFL. In one notable play, junior wide receiver Emmett Mosley got turned lose in the red zone because defenders were playing different coverages, the type of mistake that happened far too frequently late last season and contributed to the firings of coordinator Pete Kwiatkowski and defensive passing game coordinator Duane Akina.

"From a defensive perspective, as good as the day was, our ability to communicate has got to got to continue to improve. We've all got to be on the same page," Sarkisian said.

In the first scrimmage, another apparent coverage bust led to a long touchdown catch by junior wide receiver Ryan Wingo.

The communication element extends to the ability to align quickly when opponents use tempo, which happens less frequently as many offenses have gone away from the hurry-up, no-huddle approach that took college football by storm a generation ago, but every team uses situationally.

Now in the midst of mock game week, the Longhorns have survived the grind of preseason camp, and have some time to recover, but the team remains a work in progress as the nation's most difficult schedule looms.

"Fatigue makes cowards of us all, and so we've got to trust our physical and mental conditioning that we can perform under those elements and and do our job, and we didn't do it well enough Saturday to what we're capable of doing," Sarkisian said.
